# How approvals work in Casama, and what never asks

An approval system fails in two ways. Ask too often and people stop reading. Ask too rarely and the first mistake is the last time anyone trusts the bot. These are the rules we settled on.

Updated 2026-11-18. Page: https://casama.ai/blog/how-approvals-work

## Risk belongs to the action

Every tool a bot can use has a risk level: low, medium or high. Some tools work theirs out from
what they are asked to do. A shell command inside the bot's own workspace folder is low risk. The
same command deleting things outside it is high.

For apps you connect, you set the level per tool: read-only, makes changes, or always asks.

## Three settings

| Setting | The bot asks before |
|---|---|
| Ask before acting | Every action that changes something |
| Ask for risky actions | Sending email or chat messages, calling people, making a page public, deleting outside its workspace, paid data lookups, and tools marked "always asks" |
| Act on its own | Nothing, except high-risk actions on your own computer |

New bots start on the middle one. Under it a bot does most work without asking, which is the
point: an approval should mean something.

## What always asks

- **Paying with a card.** Whatever the setting. "Always allow" doesn't apply.
- **High-risk actions on your own computer.** A bot's sandbox can be restored. Your laptop can't.
- **Changing a password or two-step settings.** These are handed to you to finish.

## What never asks

A bot's notes to itself, its own routines, messages to you, tickets and checkpoints never ask.
They change only the bot's own state inside Casama, where you can see and undo them. Asking about
those would train you to tap Approve without reading.

## After a bot reads something from outside

Web pages, emails and files can contain text written to trick a bot. So the rules tighten during a
run: once a bot has read outside content, actions that send data out of Casama ask first, even
ones that normally wouldn't. That lasts until you approve something. A line in an email can't
quietly become a web request.

One more: after reading outside content, creating or changing a routine asks first. Otherwise a
web page could schedule work for later, when nobody is watching.

## What an approval looks like

A card in the chat, a "Needs you" count at the top of the app, a push notification, and buttons in
Slack. It shows the bot, the tool, its risk and exactly what it wants to do, with secrets removed.
You can approve, deny, or always allow that tool for that bot.

Deny fails only that step. The bot is told and carries on without it. No answer for 24 hours
counts as a deny. A waiting run costs nothing and survives a server restart.

## The safety net under it

Approvals depend on a person reading. So before a command that deletes data, Casama saves a
checkpoint of the bot's computer anyway. If you approve the wrong thing, you can put it back.

The full rules are in the [autonomy guide](https://docs.casama.ai/guide/autonomy), and the code
that applies them is in the [repository](https://github.com/stackwares/casama).

---

# We asked ChatGPT, Claude and Perplexity which AI agent to use

Before working on how people find Casama, we measured where things stand. We put four questions about AI agents to ChatGPT, Claude and Perplexity with web search on, and wrote down every product they named and every page they cited.

Updated 2026-11-18. Page: https://casama.ai/blog/what-ai-assistants-say-about-ai-agents

## What we asked

On November 18, 2026, through an API with web search on and the country set to the United States:

1. What are the best open-source AI agents that get their own computer and can be self-hosted?
2. I want an AI assistant that does real tasks for me on its own computer, works while I am away,
   and asks before doing anything risky. What should I use?
3. What are the best alternatives to OpenClaw?
4. Rakazo vs MausBot vs OpenBot: which AI teammate platform should I pick?

That is twelve answers. We also asked Gemini; all of its calls failed that day, so it is left out.
One run each: assistants give different lists every time, so read this as a snapshot.

## Who they named

| Question | ChatGPT | Claude | Perplexity |
|---|---|---|---|
| Open-source agents with their own computer | Hermes Agent, Agent Zero, Open WebUI | Agent Zero, Dify, OpenHands | Agent Zero |
| An assistant that works while I'm away and asks first | ChatGPT agent, OpenBot, Hermes Agent | OpenClaw, Manus, Muse, Dots | ChatGPT agent |
| Alternatives to OpenClaw | Hermes Agent, Manus | Hermes Agent, Manus | Hermes Agent, Agent Zero, n8n |
| Rakazo vs MausBot vs OpenBot | the three in the question | the three, plus Grok Bot and Lindy | the three in the question |

The table lists the names we checked for, so it is a floor, not a full count.

Casama appeared in none of the twelve. We expected that: the site was a week old.

## Three things we didn't expect

**The newest products barely register.** Rakazo, MausBot, OpenBot, Instinct and Hark Pro were
named once between them in the nine answers that didn't already mention them. Assistants reach for
the names with the most written about them: OpenClaw, Hermes Agent, Agent Zero, Manus.

**"Its own computer" isn't understood yet.** Asked for agents that get their own computer, two
assistants answered with developer frameworks and chat interfaces. The idea that an agent can have
a machine of its own, apart from yours, hasn't settled into how these models sort the field.

**Asking by name works.** Asked "What is Casama AI?", all three described it correctly, citing our
package page, our repository and our site. The assistants can find a new product. They don't yet
have a reason to bring it up.

## What they cited

Across the answers, the pages cited most were GitHub repositories, vendors' own sites, small
directories of open-source tools, community posts and roundup articles. For the three-way
comparison, the sources were the three vendors' own pages. Nobody independent had written that
comparison, so the assistants had nothing else to read.

## What we're doing about it

- Writing the comparisons that don't exist, with a source and a date on every fact about another
  product, and a section on when the other product is the better choice. They are under
  [alternatives](https://casama.ai/alternatives/).
- Explaining the idea plainly: [why give an AI agent its own computer](https://casama.ai/learn/why-give-an-ai-agent-its-own-computer).
- Repeating these questions every week and publishing how the answers change.

## Try it yourself

Ask your assistant the four questions above. If it names a product, ask it where it read that.
The sources tell you more than the answer.

# Why every Casama bot gets its own computer

The first design decision in Casama was also the most expensive one: every bot gets a computer of its own. Here is what that costs, what it buys, and why we didn't take the cheaper routes.

Updated 2026-11-18. Page: https://casama.ai/blog/why-every-bot-gets-its-own-computer

## The cheaper routes

There are three easier ways to give an AI agent somewhere to work.

**Use the person's own computer.** It is free and already signed in to everything. It also means
a model that misreads a page is one command away from your documents, and the work stops when the
lid closes.

**Use a browser session.** Light and quick to start. But a browser can't unzip a file, run a
script or keep a half-finished spreadsheet until tomorrow.

**Share one machine between all of a person's agents.** Cheaper than one each. But then the bot
that reads your mail and the bot that installs whatever a research task needs live in the same
place, with the same files and the same sign-ins.

## What one computer each buys

- **Containment.** A bot can reach only the sites and accounts you allow. A mistake stays on that
  bot's machine.
- **Continuity.** The checked-out repository, the downloaded statements and the signed-in session
  are there next time.
- **Real work.** A shell, a file system and a browser, and a full desktop when a task needs one.
- **Undo.** Before a command that deletes data, the computer is saved. Restoring puts the files
  back.
- **A window.** You can watch a bot's screen live and take over the mouse.

## What it costs, and how we pay for it

A computer that is always on is expensive. So computers sleep when a bot is idle and wake in
seconds with everything intact. On Casama Cloud, plans include a number of computer hours, and a
sleeping computer uses none. On your own server, the limit is your hardware.

The second cost is sign-ins: a new computer isn't logged in to anything. Bots get access through
the apps you connect, and logins from a password manager are filled in on the way out, for the
sites you allow, without the model seeing them.

The third is the odd website that distrusts cloud browsers. When that happens you can take over
for a moment, or lend the bot your own machine for that task, where high-risk actions always ask.

## Why not let people choose a shared machine?

Once idle computers sleep, sharing one machine saves little, and the risk is the kind you only
notice afterwards. So Casama has no setting for it.

## Where this goes

A computer per bot makes other things possible: teaching a bot by showing it a task on its
screen, bots that hand work to each other without sharing files by accident, and routines that run
at night on a machine that was asleep a minute earlier.

More on the idea: [why give an AI agent its own computer](https://casama.ai/learn/why-give-an-ai-agent-its-own-computer).

---

# Your own AI server, reachable from your phone

Self-hosting usually ends at your front door. The server runs, and then you leave the house and it might as well not exist. Casama Link is how a server on your laptop becomes an app on your phone.

Updated 2026-11-18. Page: https://casama.ai/blog/your-own-server-in-your-pocket

## The problem

Two things stop a home server from feeling like an app.

The first is the address. A machine behind a home router can't be reached from a phone on a mobile
network without a domain and port forwarding, or a VPN on every device.

The second is notifications. A phone app gets push notifications only through Apple's and
Google's services, tied to the app in the store. A server you run yourself has no way in.

## What Casama Link does

**An address.** Your server gets its own `casama.link` address over HTTPS. There is nothing to
configure on the router and no domain to buy.

**Sign-in by scanning.** The desktop app shows a QR code. Scan it with the Casama app from the
App Store or Google Play and you're signed in to your own server.

**Notifications.** When a bot needs an approval or finishes a task, the notification reaches the
store app on your phone.

## What passes through us, and what doesn't

Your bots, chats, memory and files stay on your server. Casama Cloud keeps a record of the linked
server: its name, its address and when it last checked in. It passes notifications along.

Each linked server holds one key, and what the key may do depends on how it was made. A key made
by linking can hold an address and send notifications. It can't spend credits.

## What it costs

Remote access is free on every plan, for any self-hosted server. Watching a bot's computer live
while you're away from home comes with Plus and up.

## Turning it on

From the desktop app: **Settings → Casama Link → Use on Your Phone**.

From a terminal:

```
casama selfhost remote on
```

If your server already has its own domain and you only want notifications in the store apps:

```
casama selfhost remote link
```

## The optional second half

Bot computers are the heaviest part of running Casama yourself. If your machine is small, or runs
on a platform without Docker, Casama Link can also let Casama Cloud run the bots' computers and
model calls for your server. That part is billed to a cloud workspace. Everything else stays at
home.

## Why we built it this way

The alternative was to tell self-hosters to bring a domain and a reverse proxy, and accept that
most people would never use their server from a phone. An agent you can't reach when it needs an
approval isn't much use.

Steps and details: [use your server on your phone](https://docs.casama.ai/self-hosting/remote-access).
Background: [self-hosted or hosted](https://casama.ai/learn/self-hosted-or-hosted-ai-agent).

# Starter bots

Each starter bot is a teammate with a job, a name, standing instructions and sometimes a routine. Pick one in the app and it's ready in a minute, with everything open to change.

Updated 2026-11-18. Page: https://casama.ai/bots

Every bot in Casama has its own computer, your connected apps, a memory and a schedule. A starter
bot saves you writing its instructions yourself: it comes with the job written down, a few things to
ask it first, and for some a routine, like a briefing every weekday morning. It still asks before
anything risky, such as sending, booking, paying or deleting.

To use one, open **Bots** in the app, tap **New bot** and pick it. Its name fills in, and you can
change the name, the instructions and the picture before you make it. Each one below links to its
page in the gallery, which shows what it asks for and what it can touch.

## Work

- **Dawn** (Briefing): Sends a morning briefing on topics you choose. https://gallery.casama.ai/i/bot/daily-briefing/

# Best AI agents for small business in 2026

A small business doesn't need the most powerful agent. It needs one that fits the job, the budget and the amount of setup anyone has time for. This page sorts the options by what you need done. No single product is best at everything, and that includes ours.

Updated 2026-11-18. Page: https://casama.ai/compare/best-ai-agents-for-small-business

## The short list

| If you need | Look first at |
|---|---|
| A support inbox answered, with a person approving the risky replies | Casama, Rakazo |
| The same fixed admin process run every time | n8n |
| Research and finished documents with nothing to set up | Manus |
| Shared bots for a team that lives in Slack or Teams | Grok Bot, Casama |
| The lowest cost | OpenClaw, or self-hosting Casama or Rakazo |
| Everything on your own server | OpenClaw, Casama, Rakazo |

We make Casama, so weigh our place on this list accordingly. Every fact about the others comes
from the sources at the end of the page, checked on November 18, 2026.

## Side by side

| | Casama | OpenClaw | Rakazo | Manus | Grok Bot | n8n |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Where it runs | Your own server, Mac or Linux computer, or Casama Cloud | Your own computer or server only; there is no hosted version | Your own server, a desktop app, or Rakazo's cloud | Manus's cloud; a desktop app can run commands on your computer | xAI's cloud only | Your own server, or n8n Cloud |
| A computer for the agent | Each bot has its own sandboxed Linux computer; you can watch it live and take over | Runs on your machine; a sandbox is optional and off by default | Each bot has its own container or cloud computer | A cloud sandbox with a browser, per person | One cloud computer per person, shared by all of that person's Bots | No computer per agent; agents share one code sandbox, and shell commands are self-hosted only |
| Asks before risky steps | Yes. Rules per action, risky steps wait for your OK, and a checkpoint is saved before destructive commands | Optional, and off by default | Yes: an Ask mode, or an Auto mode where a model decides when to ask | None described in the cloud; three modes on your own computer | An automatic check decides; you can add up to 20 "ask first" rules | Approve or reject on an agent's tool calls |
| Chat apps | Telegram, email, SMS, Slack, WhatsApp, Messenger, Feishu, iMessage, Microsoft Teams, Discord | About 29, including WhatsApp, Telegram, Discord, Slack, Signal, iMessage and Teams | Slack and Teams; iMessage, WhatsApp and Telegram only when self-hosted | Slack and email | X, Slack, Microsoft Teams | Slack, Telegram, Teams and Linear for agents; hundreds of apps as workflow steps |
| Teams | Workspaces with roles, group chats with people and bots, extra seats | A group that trusts each other can share one; it isn't built to separate users | Organizations, spaces and group chats; roles for people aren't described | Yes: shared credits, single sign-on, audit logs | Team Bots in Slack; admin controls on Enterprise | Users and roles; single sign-on on Enterprise or self-hosted Business |
| Price | Self-hosted: free. Cloud: Free, $15, $49 or $99 a month, credits included | Free; you pay your model provider | Self-hosted: free. Cloud: $15, $49 or $99 a month, or credits from $20 | Credits: Free; Pro from $20 a month for 4,000 credits, up to $200; Team from $20 a seat | Paid plans at $30, $100 or $200 a month; a weekly usage pool, then billed at token cost | Self-hosted Community: free. Cloud: €20 or €50 a month by executions; Business €667 |
| Free to start | Yes: a free Cloud plan, and self-hosting is free | Yes, entirely | Self-hosting is free; hosted plans have a 7-day trial | Yes: 300 credits a day | No free plan; some accounts get a 7-day trial credit | A self-hosted free edition; Cloud has a trial only |

## By what you need

### A support inbox

Support means sending messages to customers, so the question is what happens before Send. Casama
asks before sending email or chat messages under its default setting, and you can loosen that with
a rule, such as letting routine replies to your own domain go without asking. Rakazo has an Ask
mode, and an Auto mode where a model decides when to ask. OpenClaw's approvals are off until you
set them up. Manus describes none in its cloud.

Check the chat apps too. If customers write to you on WhatsApp or Telegram, look at which products
connect them on the version you plan to use. See
[AI customer support](https://casama.ai/use-cases/ai-customer-support).

### Admin and back-office work

Split admin in two. Work that follows the same steps every time, such as copying each new order
into a spreadsheet, suits n8n: you draw the workflow once and it runs the same way. Work that
changes each time, such as chasing a late invoice or filling in a supplier's web form, suits an
agent with a computer of its own. Casama, Rakazo, Manus and Grok Bot all provide one. On Grok Bot,
all of a person's Bots share that computer.

### Research

For a one-off report or a slide deck, Manus is built around finished deliverables. For a standing
job, such as a supplier price check every Monday, pick a product that starts on its own and remembers
what it learned last time. All six in the table can run on a schedule. Memory varies: Manus
projects keep instructions and files, and no separate memory is described. See
[AI research assistant](https://casama.ai/use-cases/ai-research-assistant).

### Use by a team

Ask two things: can each person have the right level of access, and what does each extra person
cost?

- **Casama** has workspaces with owner, admin and member roles. Pro includes 3 seats and Max
  includes 10, then $12 a month each.
- **Grok Bot** has team Bots in Slack, with admin controls on its Enterprise plan.
- **Manus** has team plans from $20 a seat, with shared credits, single sign-on and audit logs.
- **n8n** has users and roles.
- **Rakazo** has organizations, spaces and group chats.
- **OpenClaw** can be shared by a group that trusts each other. It isn't built to separate users.

If you are rolling agents out across a larger company, also read about
[OpenBot](https://casama.ai/alternatives/openbot), which lists roles, single sign-on, audit export and spend limits
on its paid edition.

### A tight budget

- **Free software, your own machine.** OpenClaw is free with no paid tier. Casama, Rakazo and n8n's
  Community edition are free to self-host. You still pay your model provider, unless you run a
  local model.
- **Free hosted plans.** Casama Cloud's Free plan has $1 of credits a month, 3 bots and one cloud
  computer. Manus gives 300 credits a day. Grok Bot has no free plan, n8n Cloud has a trial only,
  and Rakazo's hosted plans have a 7-day trial.
- **Paid plans.** Compare what is included, not only the price: model usage, computer hours, seats,
  and what happens when you go over.

Whichever you choose, look for a spending limit. On Casama each bot has a budget per run and per
day.

### Self-hosting

Self-hosting keeps your customers' data on a machine you control. OpenClaw, Casama, Rakazo and n8n
can all be self-hosted. Manus and Grok Bot can't. Licences differ: OpenClaw is MIT, Rakazo is
Apache-2.0, Casama is AGPL-3.0, and n8n's licence is source-available and limits use to internal, personal
or non-commercial purposes.

Someone has to look after the server. If nobody on the team is comfortable with Docker, start
hosted and move later.

## How to choose

1. **Write down one job.** "Answer support email from our help page" is a job. "Help with the
   business" is not.
2. **Decide what must wait for a person.** Refunds, payments and messages to customers are the
   usual three. Then check each product's approval row in the table.
3. **Decide who runs it.** Hosted by the vendor, or on your own server.
4. **Count the people.** One owner, or a team with different levels of access.
5. **Try the job on a free plan or a trial.** Read everything the agent did for a week before you
   let it do more.

## Where Casama fits, and where it doesn't

Casama suits a small team that wants one bot per job, each on its own computer, with risky steps
waiting for approval and a budget on each bot. Built-in personas such as Support, Sales, Ops and
Researcher give a starting point.

Its weaknesses are real. It is new, first released in November 2026, and its community is small.
It has ten chat apps, fewer than OpenClaw's 29 or so. You choose your own model only when you
self-host. If you need a fixed workflow, n8n is the better tool. If you want a deck by lunchtime
with no setup, try Manus.

## Questions

### Do I need a developer?

Not for the hosted products. Self-hosting needs someone comfortable with a server. n8n suits
someone technical who wants control of each step.

### Is it safe to give an agent our customer email?

Safer when sending waits for a person, when the agent works on a computer apart from yours, and
when you can read what it did. Start with drafts only.

### How much should we expect to pay?

From nothing beyond model usage, if you self-host, to between $15 and $200 a month for most hosted
plans in the table. n8n Cloud is €20 or €50 a month, with a Business plan at €667. Check what
happens when you use more than the plan includes.

### Can we use more than one?

Yes. A common split is a workflow builder for fixed processes and an agent for the varied work.

# Best AI personal assistants in 2026

The best AI personal assistant is the one that does your kind of task, in the places you already are, and asks before it spends money or speaks for you. This page is about assistants that act, not ones that only answer. It sorts eight of them by what you need. No single one is best at everything, and that includes ours.

Updated 2026-11-18. Page: https://casama.ai/compare/best-ai-personal-assistants

## The short list

| If you want | Look first at |
|---|---|
| A free assistant with a cloud computer of its own | Meta Muse (US only), Hark Pro, Casama |
| Nothing to install: text or call it | Instinct |
| An assistant inside a plan you already pay for | Claude Duet, ChatGPT Dots |
| Finished work, such as a trip plan or a deck, with no setup | Manus |
| The most chat apps, on your own computer, free | OpenClaw |
| Your data on your own server, with phone apps | Casama, OpenClaw |
| Firm rules about what waits for you | Claude Duet, Meta Muse, Casama |

We make Casama, so weigh our place on this list accordingly. Every fact about the others comes
from the sources at the end of the page, checked on November 18, 2026.

## By what you need

### A free plan

Meta Muse is free for most use, but only in the United States, and a card is reportedly needed to
sign up. Hark Pro's free plan includes every feature, with a usage cap it doesn't publish. Manus
gives 300 credits a day. Casama Cloud's Free plan has $1 of credits, 3 bots and one cloud computer
with 5 hours a month. OpenClaw is free software, and you pay your model provider. Claude Duet and
ChatGPT Dots come with paid plans only.

### Nothing to install

Instinct is the one you text or call like a person, with a web workspace for settings. It is
invite or waitlist only, and its price isn't published. Meta Muse also works inside WhatsApp, and
Casama bots can be reached from Telegram, WhatsApp, iMessage, SMS, email and other chat apps.

### Errands on real websites

Booking, comparing and filling in forms need a browser. Hark Pro has its own cloud browser that you
can watch. Meta Muse and Casama give the assistant a cloud computer you can watch and take over.
ChatGPT Dots each have a cloud computer you can open. Claude Duet has one you can't watch. See
[what a computer use agent is](https://casama.ai/learn/what-is-a-computer-use-agent).

### Asking before it acts

An assistant that books and pays needs firm stops. Claude Duet asks before sending, paying, signing
or deleting. Meta Muse sends email, outbound data and every purchase through a separate guard.
Casama asks before sending messages and other risky steps by default, and payments always ask.
Instinct's terms don't promise any confirmation step, and early testers reported an email sent
without permission. See [which AI agents ask before they act](https://casama.ai/learn/which-ai-agents-ask-before-they-act).

### Privacy

Hark Pro says it doesn't train on your content, and Casama doesn't use your data for training.
Instinct and Meta Muse train by default until you opt out, and Claude's consumer plans do unless
you switch it off. OpenClaw has no cloud of its own, so your model provider's policy applies. See
[which AI agents don't train on your data](https://casama.ai/learn/which-ai-agents-dont-train-on-your-data).

### Your own server

Only OpenClaw and Casama on this list can run on a machine you control. OpenClaw runs on your own
computer, with its sandbox and approvals off until you turn them on. Casama gives each bot its own
sandboxed computer on your server, and its phone apps reach that server from anywhere through
Casama Link.

## Where Casama fits, and where it doesn't

Casama suits someone who wants an assistant that keeps working when the laptop is closed, on a
computer of its own, with payments and messages waiting for approval, memory you can read and
edit, and apps on every phone and desktop.

It is new, first released in November 2026, with a small community. It reaches ten chat apps, fewer
than OpenClaw. On Casama Cloud you don't choose the model; you do when you self-host. If you want to
text an assistant with no app at all, Instinct is built for that, and if you want a free assistant
inside WhatsApp in the US, try Meta Muse.

## Questions

### What is the best free AI personal assistant?

In the US, Meta Muse has the most generous free plan for a full cloud-computer assistant. Outside
it, Hark Pro and Casama have free plans, and OpenClaw is free software you run yourself.

### Which AI personal assistant works on iPhone and Android?

Meta Muse, Hark Pro, Claude, ChatGPT, OpenClaw and Casama all have phone apps. Manus lists an iPhone
app. See [which AI agents have iPhone and Android apps](https://casama.ai/learn/which-ai-agents-have-iphone-and-android-apps).

### Can an AI personal assistant work while I'm away?

Yes, if it runs somewhere other than your phone or laptop. Hosted assistants keep working in their
cloud. A self-hosted one needs a machine that stays on. Most can also run on a schedule; see
[which AI agents run tasks on a schedule](https://casama.ai/learn/which-ai-agents-run-tasks-on-a-schedule).

### What does an AI personal assistant cost?

From nothing, on a free plan or with free software and a local model, to $20 to $200 a month for
most paid plans here. See [how much an AI agent costs](https://casama.ai/learn/how-much-does-an-ai-agent-cost).

# Best open-source AI agents in 2026

There are two kinds of open-source AI agent. Frameworks are kits for developers to build agents with. This page is about the other kind, finished agents you install and talk to. The best one for you depends on where you want it to work, your own machine or a computer of its own, and on how much setup you want to do for safety.

Updated 2026-11-18. Page: https://casama.ai/compare/best-open-source-ai-agents

## The short list

| | Best for | Stars |
|---|---|---|
| **OpenClaw** | The most chat apps, the biggest community, no paid tier at all | about 395,000 |
| **Hermes Agent** | One agent that writes its own skills and improves with use | about 264,000 |
| **nanobot** | A small Python agent in the most chat apps, including WeChat and Feishu | about 50,000 |
| **NanoClaw** | A small codebase with every session in its own container | about 31,000 |
| **MausBot** | Reusing the AI subscriptions you already pay for, on your desktop | about 24,700 |
| **Agent Zero** | A full Linux desktop for the agent, free and fully hackable | about 19,900 |
| **OpenBot** | Rolling AI coworkers out across a company with admin controls | about 12,700 |
| **Rakazo** | A computer per bot, self-hosted or hosted, with no markup on models | about 9,000 |
| **Casama** | A computer per bot with approvals on by default, native apps and a free hosted plan | new |

Star counts are from GitHub on November 18, 2026. We make Casama, so weigh our place on this list
accordingly; the other eight each have their sources at the end of the page.

## How to choose

**Where should the agent work?**

- *On my own computer.* OpenClaw, Hermes Agent, nanobot and MausBot run there by default. It is the quickest
  to set up, and the agent can reach your files and sign-ins. Turn on a sandbox if the project has
  one.
- *On a computer of its own.* Rakazo and Casama give every bot its own isolated machine by default.
  Agent Zero works in a container with its own Linux desktop, NanoClaw runs each session in a
  container, and OpenBot gives each person a container. The agent keeps working when your laptop is closed, and a
  mistake stays on its machine.

**How much do you want it to ask?**

Approvals differ more than anything else in this list. OpenClaw's are off until you configure them.
Hermes Agent asks about shell commands that match risky patterns. Agent Zero allows every tool
until you block it, nanobot has no ask step, and NanoClaw asks before installs and new tools but
not shell commands. MausBot's own site says not every
action is guaranteed to pause. OpenBot uses admin policies. Rakazo has an ask mode and an automatic
mode. Casama asks before risky actions by default, and payments always ask.

**Is it only for you?**

For a team, look at OpenBot (roles, single sign-on, audit export), Rakazo (organizations and
spaces), MausBot's paid Team plan, or Casama (workspaces with roles and group chats). OpenClaw and
Hermes Agent are built for one person or a group that trusts each other, and so are nanobot,
NanoClaw and Agent Zero.

**Do you want someone else to host it?**

Rakazo, MausBot and Casama have hosted plans at $15, $49 and $99 a month. Casama also has a free
hosted plan. Hermes Agent has an optional hosted agent through Nous Portal. OpenClaw, nanobot and Agent Zero are self-hosted only, and NanoClaw's hosted
version is invite-only.

## The nine, one by one

### OpenClaw

- You want the most chat apps: about 29 channels, plus apps on every desktop and phone platform.
- You want software with no paid tier at all, run by a nonprofit.
- You want the largest community: about 395,000 GitHub stars.

Worth knowing:

- Tools run on your own machine, and both the sandbox and approval prompts are off until you turn them on.
- The Register reported three high-impact security advisories in three days in February 2026, and malicious skills on its skill registry.
- It isn't designed for people who don't trust each other to share one agent.

### Hermes Agent

- You want one agent that teaches itself: it writes and refines its own skills and keeps searchable memory.
- You want wide model choice, including local models and several subscription sign-ins.
- You want to choose where commands run: locally, in Docker, over SSH or in a cloud sandbox.

Worth knowing:

- Commands run on your own machine by default, and its docs say the deny rules are pattern matching that scripts can get around.
- There is no phone app yet.
- It is still before version 1.0, with a very large backlog of open issues.

### nanobot

- You want an agent in many chat apps, including WeChat, Feishu, QQ and DingTalk.
- You want any model, including local ones, with fallbacks.
- You want a small Python codebase you can read, extend or embed.

Worth knowing:

- There is no hosted version: you install it, bring a model and keep it running for chat apps and schedules.
- The workspace limit and shell sandbox are off by default, and plugins run with full permissions.
- One instance has one memory and one admin, so keeping people apart takes separate instances.

### NanoClaw

- You want each agent sandboxed in its own container, with API keys kept out of it.
- You want to message your agent from many chat apps, including WhatsApp, Signal and iMessage.
- You want a small codebase you can read in an afternoon and change with a coding agent.

Worth knowing:

- It needs Docker and comfort with a terminal; there is no desktop or phone app.
- There are no settings screens: you customize it by changing code, and adding chat apps needs Claude Code.
- Containers have open internet access by default, and asking before each credential use is opt-in.

### MausBot

- You already pay for Claude Code, Codex or Grok and want to reuse those sign-ins with no markup.
- You want a free desktop app that runs bots on your own computer.
- You want many cloud computer hours for the price.

Worth knowing:

- The vendor itself says approvals aren't guaranteed to pause every action.
- Slack is the only chat app, and only on paid plans.
- Free bots stop when your computer is off, and the phone apps aren't in the stores.

### Agent Zero

- You want an agent with a full Linux desktop you can watch, including apps like LibreOffice and Blender.
- You want free software you can read and change, with plugins, MCP and A2A.
- You want to choose any model, including local ones.

Worth knowing:

- There is no hosted version: you run Docker and bring your own model keys or model server.
- Tools are allowed by default and nothing asks before acting; limits are set in agent profiles.
- No phone apps and no team accounts.

### OpenBot

- You are rolling AI coworkers out across a company and need roles, single sign-on, audit export and spend limits.
- You want to deploy inside your own cloud with Kubernetes.
- You want to plug in agents you built yourself.

Worth knowing:

- The MIT app can't run without CopilotKit Intelligence, which needs a paid licence for production.
- Only the Mac and Windows desktop apps are generally available.
- An independent review of version 1.0.2 found the default policy allows every action.

### Rakazo

- You want hosted model usage at the provider's price with no markup.
- You want a wide choice of sandbox providers for bot computers when self-hosting.
- You want every way to run it (self-hosted, desktop, hosted) from one project.

Worth knowing:

- It is young: the repository was created in August 2026 and it is before version 1.0.
- iMessage, WhatsApp and Telegram work only when self-hosted.
- The entry hosted plan has 25 computer hours a month.

### Casama

- You want each bot on its own sandboxed Linux computer that you can watch and take over.
- You want risky steps to wait for you from the start, with a checkpoint saved before destructive
  commands.
- You want native apps on iPhone, iPad, Android, Mac, Windows and Linux, and ten chat apps.
- You want a free hosted plan, or to self-host with any model.

Worth knowing:

- It is the newest here: first released in November 2026, with a small community.
- It has fewer chat apps than OpenClaw, Hermes Agent or nanobot.
- Choosing your own model is for self-hosted servers. On Casama Cloud, Casama picks.

## What about frameworks?

LangGraph, CrewAI, AutoGen and similar projects are for building your own agent in code. They are
a different choice: pick one if you are a developer with a specific product to build, and one of the
nine above if you want an agent to use this week.

## Questions

### Which open-source AI agent is the safest?

The one whose defaults match how careful you'll be. If you won't configure a sandbox and approvals
yourself, choose one where they are on from the start.

### Are these really free?

The software is. You pay for the AI model you use, unless you run a local model, and for your own
hardware. Hosted plans cost money.

### Can they run on local models?

All nine can use a local model, though NanoClaw's docs call its Ollama route a legacy workflow. Long, tool-heavy tasks
still go better on the strongest hosted models.

### Which is easiest to install?

OpenClaw, Hermes Agent, nanobot and MausBot install on a desktop with one command or a download.
Agent Zero has a desktop launcher that runs Docker for you. NanoClaw, Rakazo and Casama need
Docker, and Casama's Mac and Linux app can set it up for you.

# Casama vs Grok Bot: which should you choose?

Pick Grok Bot if you want a hosted agent from a large vendor with native apps, shared team Bots in Slack and Teams, and workflows you teach by recording them once. Pick Casama if you want open-source software, a free way to start, a separate computer for each bot, or to host it yourself.

Updated 2026-11-18. Page: https://casama.ai/compare/casama-vs-grok-bot

## The short answer

- **Grok Bot** is closed and runs only in xAI's cloud. Each person gets one cloud computer that all
  of their Bots share. You don't choose the model. Plans cost $30, $100 or $200 a month, and there
  is no free plan.
- **Casama** is open source under AGPL-3.0. Each bot gets its own sandboxed Linux computer. You
  can self-host it free with any model, or use Casama Cloud, which has a free plan.
- We make Casama, so read the table and the sources and weigh our view accordingly.

## Side by side

| | Casama | Grok Bot |
|---|---|---|
| Licence | AGPL-3.0 (SDKs and CLI Apache-2.0); a separate `ee/` folder has its own licence | Closed |
| Where it runs | Your own server, Mac or Linux computer, or Casama Cloud | xAI's cloud only |
| A computer for the agent | Each bot has its own sandboxed Linux computer; you can watch it live and take over | One cloud computer per person, shared by all of that person's Bots |
| Asks before risky steps | Yes. Rules per action, risky steps wait for your OK, and a checkpoint is saved before destructive commands | An automatic check decides; you can add up to 20 "ask first" rules |
| Choice of AI model | Any provider, a ChatGPT plan or local models when self-hosted; Casama picks on Cloud | No choice, and you aren't shown which model ran |
| Apps | iPhone, iPad, Android, Mac, Windows, Linux, web | Mac, Windows, Linux, iPhone, iPad, Android |
| Chat apps | Telegram, email, SMS, Slack, WhatsApp, Messenger, Feishu, iMessage, Microsoft Teams, Discord | X, Slack, Microsoft Teams |
| Memory | Yes, and you can read and edit it | Yes |
| Starts on its own | Schedules, webhooks, email, calendar events, check-ins | Schedules and some events |
| Teams | Workspaces with roles, group chats with people and bots, extra seats | Team Bots in Slack; admin controls on Enterprise |
| Price | Self-hosted: free. Cloud: Free, $15, $49 or $99 a month, credits included | Paid plans at $30, $100 or $200 a month; a weekly usage pool, then billed at token cost |
| Free to start | Yes: a free Cloud plan, and self-hosting is free | No free plan; some accounts get a 7-day trial credit |
| Who can use it | Open to everyone | Open; its computers run in the United States |
| Training on your data | Not used to train models | A training opt-out exists |

Facts about Grok Bot were checked on November 18, 2026. The sources are at the end of this page.

*Diagram: Two diagrams side by side. On the left, three bots all feed into one shared computer that holds one set of files and a shared setup, so what one bot does can affect the others. On the right, three bots each have their own computer with their own files and sign-ins, so each bot is walled off from the others, as in Casama.*

Bots on one shared computer share its files and setup. In Casama, each bot works on its own computer.

## Where Grok Bot wins

- You want native apps on every desktop and phone platform from a large vendor.
- You want shared team Bots in Slack and Teams with ready-made roles.
- You want to teach a workflow by recording it once.

It also reaches X, which Casama doesn't.

## Where Casama wins

- **A computer per bot.** On Grok Bot, all of a person's Bots share one computer, files and
  sign-ins. On Casama, the support bot and the research bot can't see each other's files.
- **Approvals you control.** Grok Bot uses an automatic check, plus up to 20 "ask first" rules you
  add. Casama gives every tool a risk level, lets you write rules per kind of action, and always
  asks before a payment.
- **You can see and choose the model, when self-hosted.** Grok Bot gives no choice and doesn't
  show which model ran.
- **You can host it yourself.** Grok Bot's computers run in the United States, in xAI's cloud.
  A self-hosted Casama server runs wherever you put it.
- **A free start.** Casama Cloud has a free plan and self-hosting is free. Grok Bot has no free
  plan.
- **More chat apps.** Casama has ten. Grok Bot lists X, Slack and Microsoft Teams.

## Where Casama is weaker

- It is new, first released in November 2026, and it doesn't come from a large vendor.
- Teaching by showing exists in Casama too, but only on a bot's desktop computer while you are in
  control of it. If recording workflows is the main thing you want, compare the two closely.
- On Casama Cloud you don't choose the model. That choice needs a self-hosted server.
- Its community is small, so there are fewer guides and fewer people to ask.

## Three questions to decide

1. **Do your bots need to be kept apart?** If one Bot handling everything on one computer suits
   you, Grok Bot is simpler. If different jobs should have different files, sign-ins and limits,
   Casama separates them.
2. **Do you need a fixed monthly cost?** Grok Bot has a weekly usage pool, then pay per use.
   Casama Cloud plans include dollar credits, and each bot has a budget per run and per day.
   Self-hosting costs only what your model provider charges.
3. **Does it matter where it runs?** If you need your data on your own server, or outside the
   United States, Grok Bot can't do that.

## What moving costs

**From Grok Bot to Casama.** Grok Bot has no export, so Casama asks your Bot instead: send it the
prompt from **Paste a Bot's Setup** and paste its reply into Casama. Its instructions, schedules,
skills, apps and "ask first" rules come over after you review them. Events become a note naming the
closest Casama trigger. Reconnect Slack or Teams. A workflow you taught by recording has to be taught again or described in words.

**From Casama to Grok Bot.** Your workspace exports in full, and instructions paste across. You
give up per-bot computers and self-hosting, and you start paying from the first month.

Casama's free plan lets you test one job before you cancel anything.

## Questions

### Is Grok Bot open source?

No. It is closed and can't be self-hosted. Casama is open source under AGPL-3.0, with a separate
`ee/` folder under its own licence.

### Which is cheaper?

Casama, to start: its Cloud plans are free, $15, $49 or $99 a month, and self-hosting is free.
Grok Bot starts at $30 a month. What you pay in a busy month depends on how much the bots work.

### Is my data used for training?

Grok Bot's pages say a training opt-out exists. Casama says your data is not used to train models.

### Which has better phone apps?

Both have iPhone, iPad and Android apps. Casama also has a web app.

## Sources

- Grok Bot (checked 2026-11-19): https://docs.x.ai/grok-bot/security, https://docs.x.ai/grok-bot/faq, https://docs.x.ai/grok-bot/approvals-security-and-privacy, https://x.ai/bot

More detail on the [Grok Bot alternative page](https://casama.ai/alternatives/grok-bot), or see
[all comparisons](https://casama.ai/compare/).

Join the waitlist at https://casama.ai/waitlist (Casama Cloud is invite-only for now), or run it on your own server: https://docs.casama.ai/self-hosting/

# Casama vs Hermes Agent: which should you choose?

Pick Hermes Agent if you want one agent that writes and improves its own skills, with wide model choice and a say in where its commands run. Pick Casama if you want several bots that each have their own computer, approvals for every kind of risky action, phone apps, or a workspace for a team.

Updated 2026-11-18. Page: https://casama.ai/compare/casama-vs-hermes-agent

## The short answer

- **Hermes Agent** is one agent that gets better with use. It is free and MIT-licensed, runs on
  your own computer or server, and has Mac and Windows desktop apps and a terminal app. A hosted
  agent comes with paid Nous Portal plans.
- **Casama** is a team of bots, each with its own sandboxed Linux computer, memory you can read and
  edit, and approvals on by default. It has apps on phone, desktop and web, and a free hosted plan.
- We make Casama, so read the table and the sources and weigh our view accordingly.

## Side by side

| | Casama | Hermes Agent |
|---|---|---|
| Licence | AGPL-3.0 (SDKs and CLI Apache-2.0); a separate `ee/` folder has its own licence | MIT |
| Where it runs | Your own server, Mac or Linux computer, or Casama Cloud | Your own computer or server; a hosted agent comes with paid Nous Portal plans |
| A computer for the agent | Each bot has its own sandboxed Linux computer; you can watch it live and take over | Your machine by default; Docker, SSH or cloud sandboxes are optional |
| Asks before risky steps | Yes. Rules per action, risky steps wait for your OK, and a checkpoint is saved before destructive commands | For shell commands that match risky patterns |
| Choice of AI model | Any provider, a ChatGPT plan or local models when self-hosted; Casama picks on Cloud | Your own keys, Nous Portal, some subscriptions, or local models |
| Apps | iPhone, iPad, Android, Mac, Windows, Linux, web | Mac and Windows desktop apps and a terminal app; no phone app yet |
| Chat apps | Telegram, email, SMS, Slack, WhatsApp, Messenger, Feishu, iMessage, Microsoft Teams, Discord | More than 20, including Telegram, Discord, Slack, WhatsApp, Signal, Teams and iMessage |
| Memory | Yes, and you can read and edit it | Yes, and it writes and improves its own skills |
| Starts on its own | Schedules, webhooks, email, calendar events, check-ins | Schedules set up in plain language |
| Teams | Workspaces with roles, group chats with people and bots, extra seats | Limited; separate user accounts aren't described |
| Price | Self-hosted: free. Cloud: Free, $15, $49 or $99 a month, credits included | Free; optional Nous Portal at $0, $20, $100 or $200 a month |
| Free to start | Yes: a free Cloud plan, and self-hosting is free | Yes |
| Who can use it | Open to everyone | Open to everyone |
| Training on your data | Not used to train models | With your own keys only your provider sees your data; Nous Portal may train on prompts unless Privacy Mode is on |

Facts about Hermes Agent were checked on November 18, 2026. It is still before version 1.0 and
changes quickly, so check the sources at the end for anything that matters to you.

## Where Hermes Agent wins

- You want one agent that teaches itself: it writes and refines its own skills and keeps searchable memory.
- You want wide model choice, including local models and several subscription sign-ins.
- You want to choose where commands run: locally, in Docker, over SSH or in a cloud sandbox.

It also reaches more chat apps: more than 20, including Signal, against Casama's ten.

## Where Casama wins

- **A computer per bot, by default.** Hermes Agent runs commands on your machine unless you choose
  Docker, SSH or a cloud sandbox. A Casama bot starts on its own isolated machine.
- **Approvals by kind of action, not by pattern.** Hermes Agent asks about shell commands that
  match risky patterns, and its docs say scripts can get around pattern matching. Casama gives
  every tool a risk level. Under the default setting, high-risk actions such as sending email wait
  for you, and payments always ask.
- **Phone apps.** Casama has iPhone, iPad and Android apps, with approvals as push notifications.
  Hermes Agent has no phone app yet.
- **Teams.** Casama has workspaces with roles and group chats. Hermes Agent's pages don't describe
  separate user accounts.
- **Watching and undoing.** You can watch a bot's computer live and take over, and a checkpoint is
  saved before a command that deletes data.

## Where Casama is weaker

- It is new: first released in November 2026, with a small community. Hermes Agent has about
  264,000 GitHub stars.
- It has fewer chat apps.
- Casama bots can save and improve their own skills too, and suggest new ones for you to approve,
  but self-improvement is what Hermes Agent is built around. If that is the main thing you want,
  try it first.
- You choose your own model only when you self-host. On Casama Cloud, Casama picks.

## Three questions to decide

1. **One agent or several?** If you want a single agent that learns your work over time, look at
   Hermes Agent first. If you want one bot per job, each with its own limits and budget, look at
   Casama.
2. **How much do you want it to ask?** If asking about risky shell commands is enough, Hermes
   Agent does that. If you want sending, publishing and paying to wait for you too, Casama does
   that from the start.
3. **Where will you use it?** At a desk or in a terminal, either works. From your phone, or with
   colleagues, Casama fits better today.

## What moving costs

**From Hermes Agent to Casama.** Casama imports a Hermes Agent home folder: pick the folder in the
desktop app, or upload a ZIP of it. Its persona, memories, skills and scheduled jobs come over, and
you review each one first. Keys and settings files are never read. See
[Import an agent](https://docs.casama.ai/guide/sharing#import-an-agent). Reconnect chat apps, and check yours are
among Casama's ten. Self-hosting needs Docker. Casama Cloud needs nothing installed.

**From Casama to Hermes Agent.** Your workspace exports in full, and instructions are plain text.
You give up the per-bot computers, phone apps and workspace roles, and you choose and set up where
commands run.

Both are free to run yourself, so a side-by-side week costs only model usage.

## Questions

### Which has better model choice?

Hermes Agent, if you count the hosted option: it takes your own keys, Nous Portal, some
subscriptions and local models. Self-hosted Casama takes any provider, a ChatGPT plan or local
models, but Casama Cloud picks the model for you.

### Is either one free?

Both are free to self-host. Casama Cloud has a free plan. Nous Portal has a $0 tier and paid
plans.

### Which is safer?

Neither is safe without attention. The difference is the starting point: Hermes Agent runs on your
machine by default, and Casama bots run on their own machines with approvals on.

### Can I run both?

Yes. They don't conflict.

More detail on the [Hermes Agent alternative page](https://casama.ai/alternatives/hermes-agent), or see
[all comparisons](https://casama.ai/compare/).

# Casama vs Manus: which should you choose?

Pick Manus if you want a hosted agent with nothing to set up that hands back finished deliverables such as slide decks, websites and wide research. Pick Casama if you want open-source software you can run yourself, approvals before risky steps, standing bots with their own memory, or more chat apps.

Updated 2026-11-18. Page: https://casama.ai/compare/casama-vs-manus

## The short answer

- **Manus** is a closed, hosted agent. It works in a cloud sandbox with a browser, and a desktop
  app can run commands on your computer. Manus picks the model. Plans are priced in credits.
- **Casama** is open source under AGPL-3.0. Each bot has its own sandboxed Linux computer, asks
  before risky steps, and keeps memory you can read and edit. You can self-host it free or use
  Casama Cloud.
- We make Casama, so read the table and the sources and weigh our view accordingly.

## Side by side

| | Casama | Manus |
|---|---|---|
| Licence | AGPL-3.0 (SDKs and CLI Apache-2.0); a separate `ee/` folder has its own licence | Closed |
| Where it runs | Your own server, Mac or Linux computer, or Casama Cloud | Manus's cloud; a desktop app can run commands on your computer |
| A computer for the agent | Each bot has its own sandboxed Linux computer; you can watch it live and take over | A cloud sandbox with a browser, per person |
| Asks before risky steps | Yes. Rules per action, risky steps wait for your OK, and a checkpoint is saved before destructive commands | None described in the cloud; three modes on your own computer |
| Choice of AI model | Any provider, a ChatGPT plan or local models when self-hosted; Casama picks on Cloud | Manus picks; no choice on standard plans |
| Apps | iPhone, iPad, Android, Mac, Windows, Linux, web | Web, iPhone, iPad, Mac (Apple silicon), Windows |
| Chat apps | Telegram, email, SMS, Slack, WhatsApp, Messenger, Feishu, iMessage, Microsoft Teams, Discord | Slack and email |
| Memory | Yes, and you can read and edit it | Projects keep instructions and files; no separate memory is described |
| Starts on its own | Schedules, webhooks, email, calendar events, check-ins | Schedules and events: 2 on Free, 20 on Pro |
| Teams | Workspaces with roles, group chats with people and bots, extra seats | Yes: shared credits, single sign-on, audit logs |
| Price | Self-hosted: free. Cloud: Free, $15, $49 or $99 a month, credits included | Credits: Free; Pro from $20 a month for 4,000 credits, up to $200; Team from $20 a seat |
| Free to start | Yes: a free Cloud plan, and self-hosting is free | Yes: 300 credits a day |
| Who can use it | Open to everyone | Open; sales were paused in some regions in August 2026 |
| Training on your data | Not used to train models | Team plans say no; individual plans are unclear |

Facts about Manus were checked on November 18, 2026. The sources are at the end of this page.

## Where Manus wins

- You want nothing to set up: a hosted agent with its own cloud computer on web, phone and desktop.
- You want finished deliverables such as slide decks, websites and wide research.
- You want team administration on a hosted product.

Its team plan also lists shared credits, single sign-on and audit logs. On Casama, single sign-on
and audit-log export are in the separately licensed `ee/` folder.

## Where Casama wins

- **You can run it yourself.** Casama's code is open and self-hosting is free, with no limit on
  users or bots. Manus is closed and runs in its own cloud.
- **Approvals.** Under the default setting, a Casama bot asks before sending email or chat
  messages, making a page public and other high-risk actions. Payments always ask. Manus's pages
  describe no approvals for its cloud, and three modes when it works on your own computer.
- **Model choice when self-hosted.** Any provider, a ChatGPT plan or local models. Manus gives no
  choice on standard plans.
- **Chat apps.** Casama has ten. Manus lists Slack and email.
- **Memory.** Each Casama bot keeps memory you can read and edit. Manus projects keep instructions
  and files, and no separate memory is described.
- **Spending you can predict.** On Casama Cloud a credit is a dollar, each bot has a budget per run
  and per day, and each reply shows what it cost.

## Where Casama is weaker

- It is new: first released in November 2026, with a small community.
- Manus's strength is the finished deliverable. If a polished slide deck is the whole job, try
  Manus first.
- On Casama Cloud you don't choose the model either. Choice comes with self-hosting.
- Self-hosting is work. Manus needs no setup at all.

## Three questions to decide

1. **Does it matter who runs it?** If your data must stay on a machine you control, or you want to
   read the code, only Casama fits. If hosted by the vendor is fine, both do.
2. **Do you want one-off deliverables or standing jobs?** For "make me this deck", Manus is built
   for it. For a support bot or a research bot that works every day and remembers how you like
   things, Casama is built for it.
3. **How much should it ask?** If it will send mail or spend money, check how each product
   handles that before you connect anything.

## What moving costs

**From Manus to Casama.** We haven't confirmed an export tool on Manus's side, so plan to copy by
hand. Take each project's instructions and files, create a bot for each standing job, and paste
the instructions in. Recreate scheduled tasks as routines. Unused Manus credits don't come with
you.

**From Casama to Manus.** Your workspace exports in full. Instructions paste across. You give up
self-hosting, per-bot computers and the approval rules you wrote.

Both have a free way to start: Manus gives 300 credits a day, and Casama Cloud's Free plan has $1
of credits a month. Try the same task on each before paying.

## Questions

### Is Manus open source?

No. Manus is closed. Casama is open source under AGPL-3.0, with a separate `ee/` folder under its
own licence.

### Which is cheaper?

It depends on the work. Manus Pro starts at $20 a month for 4,000 credits, and credit use depends
on how complex a task turns out to be. Casama Cloud is free, $15, $49 or $99 a month with dollar
credits included, and self-hosting is free.

### Is Manus available everywhere?

Manus says it paused sales in some regions in August 2026. Check its help pages for your country.
Casama is open to everyone.

### Can Casama make slide decks and websites?

A Casama bot can make documents, pages and sites on its computer and keep them in the Library. We
make no claim that the results match Manus's.

## Sources

- Manus (checked 2026-11-18): https://manus.im, https://manus.im/docs/features/desktop.md, https://manus.im/docs/introduction/welcome.md, https://manus.im/team, https://apps.apple.com/us/app/manus-ai-agent-automation/id6740909540, https://manus.im/docs/llms.txt, https://help.manus.im/en/articles/11711111-what-is-the-current-membership-pricing-for-manus, https://help.manus.im/en/articles/11711097-what-are-the-pricing-plans, https://help.manus.im/en/articles/16147831-service-change-overview-what-s-happening-and-am-i-affected

[all comparisons](https://casama.ai/compare/).

# Casama vs n8n: which should you choose?

These are different tools. Pick n8n if you can draw the process as a flowchart and want it to run the same way every time. Pick Casama if the work changes each time, needs judgement or a web browser, and you would rather describe the outcome than build the steps. Many teams will want both.

Updated 2026-11-18. Page: https://casama.ai/compare/casama-vs-n8n

## The short answer

- **n8n** is a workflow builder. You connect steps in a visual editor, and it has hundreds of
  ready-made app connections. It runs on your own server or n8n Cloud. Its licence is
  source-available, not open source.
- **Casama** is a team of bots. You tell a bot what you want in plain words, and it works out the
  steps on its own sandboxed Linux computer, with a browser, files and a shell. It is open source
  under AGPL-3.0.
- We make Casama, so read the table and the sources and weigh our view accordingly.

## Side by side

| | Casama | n8n |
|---|---|---|
| Licence | AGPL-3.0 (SDKs and CLI Apache-2.0); a separate `ee/` folder has its own licence | Sustainable Use License: source-available, not open source; for internal, personal or non-commercial use |
| Where it runs | Your own server, Mac or Linux computer, or Casama Cloud | Your own server, or n8n Cloud |
| A computer for the agent | Each bot has its own sandboxed Linux computer; you can watch it live and take over | No computer per agent; agents share one code sandbox, and shell commands are self-hosted only |
| Asks before risky steps | Yes. Rules per action, risky steps wait for your OK, and a checkpoint is saved before destructive commands | Approve or reject on an agent's tool calls |
| Choice of AI model | Any provider, a ChatGPT plan or local models when self-hosted; Casama picks on Cloud | Many providers with your own keys, or local models through Ollama |
| Apps | iPhone, iPad, Android, Mac, Windows, Linux, web | A web editor; no desktop app |
| Chat apps | Telegram, email, SMS, Slack, WhatsApp, Messenger, Feishu, iMessage, Microsoft Teams, Discord | Slack, Telegram, Teams and Linear for agents; hundreds of apps as workflow steps |
| Memory | Yes, and you can read and edit it | Yes, across sessions for agents |
| Starts on its own | Schedules, webhooks, email, calendar events, check-ins | Schedules and app triggers |
| Teams | Workspaces with roles, group chats with people and bots, extra seats | Users and roles; single sign-on on Enterprise or self-hosted Business |
| Price | Self-hosted: free. Cloud: Free, $15, $49 or $99 a month, credits included | Self-hosted Community: free. Cloud: €20 or €50 a month by executions; Business €667 |
| Free to start | Yes: a free Cloud plan, and self-hosting is free | A self-hosted free edition; Cloud has a trial only |
| Who can use it | Open to everyone | Open to everyone |
| Training on your data | Not used to train models | Says assistant data isn't used to train AI providers' models |

Facts about n8n were checked on November 18, 2026. The sources are at the end of this page.

## Where n8n wins

- You want to build exact, repeatable workflows step by step in a visual editor.
- You need hundreds of ready-made app connections.
- You have someone technical who wants full control of each step.

A workflow you drew does the same thing on every run. A bot decides its steps each time, which is
the wrong trade for a process that must never vary, such as copying every paid invoice into a
spreadsheet.

## Where Casama wins

- **Work you can't draw.** "Find three suppliers and compare their terms" has no fixed path. A bot
  can search, read and decide as it goes.
- **A real computer.** A Casama bot has its own machine with a browser, so it can use sites that
  have no API and handle files. n8n agents share one code sandbox and don't get a computer each.
- **Nothing to build.** You describe the job. There is no canvas to maintain when an input
  changes shape.
- **Apps on phone and desktop.** Casama has native apps, with approvals as push notifications.
  n8n is a web editor.
- **Licence and free hosting.** Casama is open source (AGPL-3.0) and has a free Cloud plan. n8n's licence
  limits use to internal, personal or non-commercial purposes, and n8n Cloud has a trial only.

## Where Casama is weaker

- It is new: first released in November 2026, with a small community.
- Its own app catalog is much smaller than n8n's hundreds of ready-made connections. Other apps
  come through connector services or any MCP server, which is more setup.
- A bot's run is less predictable than a workflow, and each step uses a model, so a simple fixed
  job can cost more on Casama than on n8n.
- You choose your own model only when you self-host. On Casama Cloud, Casama picks.

## Three questions to decide

1. **Can you write the task as a flowchart?** If yes, n8n will run it reliably. If every case is a
   little different, a bot fits better.
2. **Who will look after it?** n8n suits someone technical who wants control of each step. Casama
   suits someone who wants to hand the job over in a sentence and review the result.
3. **Does the task need a browser or files?** If it means signing in to a website and clicking
   through it, a bot with its own computer can do that.

## Using both

They work together. A Casama routine can start from a webhook, so an n8n workflow can hand a messy
step to a bot. And a bot can make web requests, so it can start an n8n workflow when a task reaches
a step that should always run the same way.

## What moving costs

Don't move the workflows that work. Moving is a rewrite, not an import: a workflow is a diagram
and a routine is a paragraph of instructions.

**From n8n to Casama.** Pick the workflows you keep patching because the inputs vary. Describe
each as a routine for a bot, such as "every weekday at 8, read the support inbox and draft replies
from the help docs". Connect the same apps. Keep approvals on, and compare the results with the
old workflow for a week or two.

**From Casama to n8n.** When a routine turns out to do the same steps every time, it is a good
candidate to rebuild as a workflow. You draw the steps the bot was taking.

## Questions

### Is n8n open source?

Not in the usual sense. Its code is public under the Sustainable Use License, which limits use to
internal, personal or non-commercial purposes. Casama is open source under AGPL-3.0, with a separate `ee/` folder
under its own licence.

### Which is cheaper?

Self-hosted, both are free. n8n Cloud costs €20 or €50 a month, priced by executions. Casama Cloud
is free, $15, $49 or $99 a month, priced by credits.

### Does n8n have AI agents?

Yes. n8n agents have memory across sessions and approve or reject steps on their tool calls. They
don't get a computer of their own.

### Do Casama bots ask before acting?

Yes. Under the default setting they ask before high-risk actions such as sending email, and
payments always ask.

## Sources

- n8n (checked 2026-11-18): https://docs.n8n.io/n8n-community-license/community-license.md, https://docs.n8n.io/choose-n8n/, https://docs.n8n.io/build/build-and-manage-agents.md, https://docs.n8n.io/build/integrate-ai/ai-examples/human-in-the-loop-for-tools.md, https://docs.n8n.io/llms.txt, https://community.n8n.io/t/sunsetting-self-hosted-team-plan-desktop-version/25830, https://docs.n8n.io/build/integrate-ai/understand-ai-components/how-memory-works.md, https://docs.n8n.io/integrations/builtin/core-nodes/n8n-nodes-base.scheduletrigger.md, https://n8n.io/pricing/, https://docs.n8n.io/privacy-and-security/privacy.md

More detail on the [n8n alternative page](https://casama.ai/alternatives/n8n), or see
[all comparisons](https://casama.ai/compare/).

Join the waitlist at https://casama.ai/waitlist (Casama Cloud is invite-only for now), or run it on your own server: https://docs.casama.ai/self-hosting/

# Casama vs OpenClaw: which should you choose?

Pick OpenClaw if you want one free agent on your own machine, reachable from about 29 chat apps, and you are happy to set up its safety features yourself. Pick Casama if you want each bot on a computer of its own, approvals on from the first day, room for a team, or a hosted plan.

Updated 2026-11-18. Page: https://casama.ai/compare/casama-vs-openclaw

## The short answer

- **OpenClaw** is one agent on your own computer or server. It is free, MIT-licensed, has no paid
  tier and no hosted version, and connects to about 29 chat apps.
- **Casama** is a team of bots. Each one has its own sandboxed Linux computer, asks before risky
  steps by default, and can be shared in a workspace with roles. You can self-host it free or use
  Casama Cloud.
- We make Casama, so read the table and the sources and weigh our view accordingly.

## Side by side

| | Casama | OpenClaw |
|---|---|---|
| Licence | AGPL-3.0 (SDKs and CLI Apache-2.0); a separate `ee/` folder has its own licence | MIT |
| Where it runs | Your own server, Mac or Linux computer, or Casama Cloud | Your own computer or server only; there is no hosted version |
| A computer for the agent | Each bot has its own sandboxed Linux computer; you can watch it live and take over | Runs on your machine; a sandbox is optional and off by default |
| Asks before risky steps | Yes. Rules per action, risky steps wait for your OK, and a checkpoint is saved before destructive commands | Optional, and off by default |
| Choice of AI model | Any provider, a ChatGPT plan or local models when self-hosted; Casama picks on Cloud | Your own keys, a ChatGPT or Claude plan, or local models |
| Apps | iPhone, iPad, Android, Mac, Windows, Linux, web | Mac, Windows, Linux, iPhone, Android; no hosted web app |
| Chat apps | Telegram, email, SMS, Slack, WhatsApp, Messenger, Feishu, iMessage, Microsoft Teams, Discord | About 29, including WhatsApp, Telegram, Discord, Slack, Signal, iMessage and Teams |
| Memory | Yes, and you can read and edit it | Yes, as Markdown files on your disk |
| Starts on its own | Schedules, webhooks, email, calendar events, check-ins | Schedules, event triggers, webhooks |
| Teams | Workspaces with roles, group chats with people and bots, extra seats | A group that trusts each other can share one; it isn't built to separate users |
| Price | Self-hosted: free. Cloud: Free, $15, $49 or $99 a month, credits included | Free; you pay your model provider |
| Free to start | Yes: a free Cloud plan, and self-hosting is free | Yes, entirely |
| Who can use it | Open to everyone | Open to everyone |
| Training on your data | Not used to train models | There is no OpenClaw cloud; your model provider's policy applies |

Facts about OpenClaw were checked on November 18, 2026. It ships new versions most weeks, so check
the sources at the end for anything that matters to you.

## Where OpenClaw wins

- You want the most chat apps: about 29 channels, plus apps on every desktop and phone platform.
- You want software with no paid tier at all, run by a nonprofit.
- You want the largest community: about 395,000 GitHub stars.

It is also the simpler thing to reason about: one agent, on the machine in front of you, with your
own model keys, a ChatGPT or Claude plan, or local models.

## Where Casama wins

- **A computer per bot.** Each bot works on an isolated Linux machine, apart from your own files.
  OpenClaw's sandbox is optional and off by default.
- **Approvals from the start.** Under the default setting a bot asks before sending email or chat
  messages, making a page public and other high-risk actions. Payments always ask. OpenClaw's
  approval prompts are off until you configure them.
- **An undo.** A checkpoint of the bot's computer is saved before a shell command that deletes data.
- **More than one person.** Workspaces have owner, admin and member roles. OpenClaw's docs say it
  isn't built to separate users.
- **A hosted option.** Casama Cloud has a free plan. OpenClaw is self-hosted only.

## Where Casama is weaker

- It is new: first released in November 2026, with a far smaller community than OpenClaw's roughly
  395,000 GitHub stars.
- It has ten chat apps, not 29. Signal is on OpenClaw's list and not on Casama's.
- You choose your own model only when you self-host. On Casama Cloud, Casama picks.
- Hosted plans beyond the free one cost money. OpenClaw has nothing to pay for except your model
  provider.

## Three questions to decide

1. **Where should the agent work?** If you want it on your own machine, with your files and
   sign-ins to hand, OpenClaw does that by default. If you want it kept away from them, Casama
   does that by default.
2. **Will you set up the sandbox and approvals yourself?** If yes, OpenClaw gives you the controls.
   If you would rather they were on already, choose Casama.
3. **Is it only for you?** For one person, or a group that trusts each other fully, either works.
   For a team with different levels of access, Casama has roles and workspaces.

## What moving costs

**From OpenClaw to Casama.** Casama imports an OpenClaw folder: pick it in the desktop app, or
upload a ZIP. Its persona, memories, skills and scheduled jobs come over, and you review each one
first. Keys and settings files are never read. See
[Import an agent](https://docs.casama.ai/guide/sharing#import-an-agent). Reconnect each chat app per bot, and check first that the ones you use are among Casama's ten.
Self-hosting needs a server or computer that runs Docker. Casama Cloud needs nothing installed.

**From Casama to OpenClaw.** Your workspace exports in full, and instructions and schedules are
plain text you can paste across. You give up the per-bot computers and workspace roles, and you
take on turning the sandbox and approvals on.

You don't have to move at once. Both are free to run, so you can try one job on each for a week.

## Questions

### Is Casama a fork of OpenClaw?

No. They are separate projects with different designs and licences: OpenClaw is MIT, Casama is
AGPL-3.0 with a separate `ee/` folder under its own licence.

### Which is safer?

It depends on setup. OpenClaw can be set up carefully, but its docs say the sandbox and approval
prompts are off until you turn them on. Casama starts with both on. Neither removes the need to
read what your agent does.

### Which is cheaper?

Self-hosted, both are free and you pay your model provider. If you want hosting, only Casama
offers it, from a free plan up to $99 a month.

### Can I use local models with both?

Yes. Both accept local models when you run them yourself.

More detail on the [OpenClaw alternative page](https://casama.ai/alternatives/openclaw), or see
[all comparisons](https://casama.ai/compare/).

Join the waitlist at https://casama.ai/waitlist (Casama Cloud is invite-only for now), or run it on your own server: https://docs.casama.ai/self-hosting/
