# How much does an AI agent cost a month?

Using an AI agent costs from nothing, with free software and a local model, to between $15 and $200 a month for most hosted plans. You pay for three things: the software, the AI model and the computer it works on. Hosted plans bundle all three, usually with a usage limit. Open-source agents make the software free and leave the model bill to you.

Updated 2026-11-18. Page: https://casama.ai/learn/how-much-does-an-ai-agent-cost

## What you pay for

| Part | What it is | How it's billed |
|---|---|---|
| The software | The agent itself | Free if open source; a subscription if hosted |
| The model | Every step is a call to an AI model | Per use with your own key, inside a plan's credits, or free with a local model |
| The computer | Somewhere for the agent to work, often with a browser | Your own machine, or hours included in a hosted plan |

This page is about using an agent. Building a custom agent with a developer is a different budget,
priced as a project.

## Published prices

| Agent | Price | Free to start |
|---|---|---|
| **Casama** | Self-hosted: free. Cloud: Free, $15, $49 or $99 a month, credits included | Yes: a free Cloud plan, and self-hosting is free |
| **OpenClaw** | Free; you pay your model provider | Yes, entirely |
| **Hermes Agent** | Free; optional Nous Portal at $0, $20, $100 or $200 a month | Yes |
| **Agent Zero** | Free; you pay your model provider | Yes, all of it |
| **NanoClaw** | Free; you pay your model provider | Yes, all of it |
| **nanobot** | Free; you pay your model provider | Yes, all of it |
| **Rakazo** | Self-hosted: free. Cloud: $15, $49 or $99 a month, or credits from $20 | Self-hosting is free; hosted plans have a 7-day trial |
| **MausBot** | Desktop app: free. Cloud: $15, $49 or $99 a month; Team $40 for two people | Yes, the desktop app |
| **OpenBot** | Free for personal use; Business up to $29 per active user a month | Yes, for one person on their own laptop |
| **n8n** | Self-hosted Community: free. Cloud: €20 or €50 a month by executions; Business €667 | A self-hosted free edition; Cloud has a trial only |
| **Manus** | Credits: Free; Pro from $20 a month for 4,000 credits, up to $200; Team from $20 a seat | Yes: 300 credits a day |
| **Grok Bot** | Paid plans at $30, $100 or $200 a month; a weekly usage pool, then billed at token cost. [Details](https://casama.ai/compare/grok-bot-pricing) | No free plan; some accounts get a 7-day trial credit |
| **Hark Pro** | Free; $20 or $100 a month for more usage | Yes, with every feature; the cap isn't published |
| **Meta Muse** | Free for most use; paid plans add usage (reported at $20 and $100 a month) | Yes; a card is reportedly needed to sign up |
| **Lindy** | From $29.99 a month per seat for 3,000 credits; Enterprise custom | $50 of credits for 7 days |
| **Claude Cowork and Duet** | Included in paid Claude plans and counted against their limits | No |
| **ChatGPT Dots** | One dot is included with ChatGPT Pro and Business Premium | No |

Checked on November 18, 2026, from each product's pricing page; the sources are at the end.
Instinct hasn't published a price. We make Casama.

## Why the sticker price isn't the cost

Two plans at the same price can buy very different amounts of work. Before you compare, find out:

- **What a credit is.** On some products a credit's worth depends on how complex a task turns out
  to be, so you can't price a task in advance. On Casama Cloud a credit is a dollar.
- **How many computer hours you get.** Rakazo's entry plan has 25 a month. Casama's plans include
  5, 30, 100 or 300 hours.
- **What happens at the limit.** Does it stop, wait for next week, or start charging? Grok Bot
  moves to pay per use after its weekly pool.
- **Whether waiting costs money.** An agent waiting for your approval shouldn't be burning hours.
- **How many people.** Per-seat pricing adds up fast for a team.

## The cheapest way to run one

1. Install an open-source agent on a computer you already own.
2. Use a local model for routine work; nothing is billed.
3. Add your own API key for the hard tasks, and set a spending limit with the provider.

The catch is the time it takes to set up and look after, and a machine that has to stay on. See
[are there free AI agents](https://casama.ai/learn/are-there-free-ai-agents).

## What Casama costs

- **Free**: $0. $1 of credits a month, 3 bots, 1, with 5 hours, Included Library, 1.
- **Plus**: $15 a month, or $150 a year. $5 of credits a month, 10 bots, 2, with 30 hours, 10 GB Library, 1.
- **Pro**: $49 a month, or $490 a year. $15 of credits a month, Unlimited bots, 5, with 100 hours, 50 GB Library, 3, then $12 each.
- **Max**: $99 a month, or $899 a year. $30 of credits a month, Unlimited bots, 10, with 300 hours, 200 GB Library, 10, then $12 each.

- **Self-hosted Casama is free**, with no limit on users, bots or computers. You pay your model
  providers directly, and local models cost nothing.
- **Each bot has a budget** per run ($1 by default) and per day ($10 by default). At the limit, the
  run stops and tells you.
- **A run waiting for your approval costs nothing.**
- **When credits run out**, bots stop starting new paid work until next month or until you buy a
  credit pack. Nothing is charged without you choosing it.

Each reply shows what it cost. See [pricing](https://casama.ai/pricing).

## Questions

### What does an AI agent with its own cloud computer cost?

Hosted plans that include one start free with limited hours: Casama's Free plan includes 5 hours a
month and Manus gives 300 credits a day. Paid plans run from $15 to $200 a month. Self-hosted, the
computer runs on your own server.

### Is an AI agent cheaper than a virtual assistant?

It can be, for routine work done on a screen, but it needs checking and can't do everything a
person can. Price one specific job both ways, including the time you spend reviewing.

### How do I keep an AI agent from running up a bill?

Use a spending limit at every layer: a budget per agent if it has one, a cap with your model
provider, and a plan that stops at its limit instead of charging more.

# How do I self-host an AI agent?

You need a machine with Docker, a key for an AI model or a local model, and about 15 minutes. Install the server with one command, sign in, add a model, and give your first bot a task.

Updated 2026-11-18. Page: https://casama.ai/learn/how-to-self-host-an-ai-agent

## What you need

- **A machine with Docker**: a VPS, a home server, or your own Mac, Windows or Linux computer.
- **A model**: an API key from a provider such as Anthropic, OpenAI or Google, a ChatGPT plan, or a
  local model running in Ollama.
- **Optional: a domain**, if other people will reach the server over the internet.

*Diagram: Two columns comparing Casama Cloud with self-hosted Casama. Casama Cloud: Casama runs the servers and computers, Casama picks and runs the models, you pay with credits, and you just sign up and start. Self-hosted: your own server or Mac runs everything, you use your own model keys or local models, it is free to run, and you update and back up yourself.*

Casama Cloud is run for you and paid in credits; self-hosted is free to run on your own machine with your own models.

## The steps

These use Casama, which is open source and free to self-host. Other self-hosted agents follow the
same outline.

### 1. Install the server

To try it on your own computer:

```
git clone https://github.com/stackwares/casama && cd casama
./install.sh --local
```

For a server on the internet, point a domain at the machine first, then:

```
./install.sh --domain casama.example.com
```

The installer checks Docker, creates every secret, starts the stack and waits until it is healthy.
It prints the address when it is done.

### 2. Sign in

Open the address in a browser, or install the Casama app and enter the server's address. The first
person to sign up owns the server.

### 3. Add a model

In settings, add a model key, sign in with your ChatGPT plan, or enter the address of a local
model, for example `http://127.0.0.1:11434/v1` for Ollama on the same machine.

### 4. Meet your first bot

A short welcome chat sets up your first bot. Ask it for something real: "find the three best-rated
ramen places near me and put them in a table".

### 5. Reach it from your phone

A server installed with `--local` answers only on that computer. Turn on Casama Link and it gets
an address your phone can reach from anywhere, free, with no domain and no open ports. Scan a code
with the app to sign in.

## No terminal?

The Casama desktop app for Mac and Linux can run the server for you: start Docker Desktop, then
choose **Run Casama on This Computer** on the sign-in screen. It needs about 10 GB of free disk.

## After it's running

| Job | How |
|---|---|
| Update | Pull the new version and run the installer again |
| Back up | Back up the database and the data folder; the docs list what to keep |
| Add people | Invite them from settings; there is no limit on users |
| Watch costs | The Usage screen shows spend by bot and model. Local models are recorded at $0 |
| Add tools | Connect apps, install skills from the gallery, or add MCP servers |

The [self-hosting guide](https://docs.casama.ai/self-hosting/) covers requirements, every option,
production advice and troubleshooting.

## Common problems

- **Docker isn't running.** Start Docker Desktop, or the Docker service on Linux, and run the
  installer again.
- **The phone app can't find the server.** A `--local` server isn't reachable from outside. Use
  Casama Link or a domain.
- **A local model is slow or forgets tools.** Use a larger model, or keep a hosted model as the
  bot's fallback.

## Related questions

- [Self-hosted or hosted AI agent: which should I choose?](https://casama.ai/learn/self-hosted-or-hosted-ai-agent)
- [How do I run AI agents on my own server from my phone?](https://casama.ai/learn/run-ai-agents-on-your-own-server-from-your-phone)

Join the waitlist at https://casama.ai/waitlist (Casama Cloud is invite-only for now), or run it on your own server: https://docs.casama.ai/self-hosting/

# AI agents, explained

Short, plain answers to the questions people ask before they hand work to an AI agent.

Updated 2026-11-18. Page: https://casama.ai/learn/

- [AI agent vs chatbot: what's the difference?](https://casama.ai/learn/ai-agent-vs-chatbot.md): A chatbot answers in a text box. An AI agent has tools, a place to work, memory and a schedule, so it does the task itself. A side-by-side table.
- [Are there free AI agents?](https://casama.ai/learn/are-there-free-ai-agents.md): Yes. Open-source AI agents are free to run and some hosted ones have free plans, but the AI model usually costs money unless you run one locally.
- [Can AI agents run on my own models?](https://casama.ai/learn/can-ai-agents-run-on-local-models.md): Yes. An AI agent can use a local model through Ollama, LM Studio or vLLM if the agent software accepts an OpenAI-style endpoint. What works and what doesn't.
- [How do AI agents work?](https://casama.ai/learn/how-do-ai-agents-work.md): An AI agent runs a loop: the model picks a step, a tool carries it out, the model reads the result and picks the next step, until the task is done.
- [How much does an AI agent cost a month?](https://casama.ai/learn/how-much-does-an-ai-agent-cost.md): From $0 for free software and a local model, to $15 to $200 a month for most hosted AI agents. What you pay for, and the published prices of 17 agents.
- [How do I self-host an AI agent?](https://casama.ai/learn/how-to-self-host-an-ai-agent.md): To self-host an AI agent you need a machine with Docker, an AI model key or a local model, and about 15 minutes. The steps, with Casama as the example.
- [Is it safe to give an AI agent access to my email and accounts?](https://casama.ai/learn/is-it-safe-to-give-an-ai-agent-access-to-my-email.md): It can be, if the agent asks before sending, can't see your passwords, treats message content as untrusted, and you can see and undo what it did.
- [Is OpenClaw safe, and is it free?](https://casama.ai/learn/is-openclaw-safe.md): OpenClaw is free and MIT-licensed. It can be run safely, but its sandbox and approvals are off by default. What that means, and how to set it up more safely.
- [How do I run AI agents on my own server from my phone?](https://casama.ai/learn/run-ai-agents-on-your-own-server-from-your-phone.md): Run the agent software on a computer at home, give it an address your phone can reach without port forwarding, and sign in with a native app.
- [Self-hosted or hosted AI agent: which should you choose?](https://casama.ai/learn/self-hosted-or-hosted-ai-agent.md): Host it yourself for control over data, models and cost. Use a hosted agent for no setup and no upkeep. A table of trade-offs and a way to decide.
- [What is a computer use agent, and which ones let you take over?](https://casama.ai/learn/what-is-a-computer-use-agent.md): A computer use agent works a computer like you do: screen, mouse, keyboard, browser. Where it runs, why it matters, and which agents let you take over.
- [What is an AI agent?](https://casama.ai/learn/what-is-an-ai-agent.md): An AI agent is software that uses an AI model to do a task step by step with tools, not just answer. Examples, limits and how it differs from a chatbot.
- [What is an AI employee?](https://casama.ai/learn/what-is-an-ai-employee.md): An AI employee is an AI agent given a standing job, with tools, memory, a schedule and limits. What AI workers can do, what they cost, and where they fail.
- [What is an AI teammate?](https://casama.ai/learn/what-is-an-ai-teammate.md): An AI teammate is an AI agent that stays: it has a role, remembers your work, starts tasks without being asked and works alongside people.
- [What is MCP, and what is an MCP client?](https://casama.ai/learn/what-is-mcp.md): MCP (Model Context Protocol) is a standard way for AI apps to use outside tools and data. A server offers tools; a client is the AI app that uses them.
- [Which AI agents ask before they act?](https://casama.ai/learn/which-ai-agents-ask-before-they-act.md): Most AI agents ask before some actions. They differ in which actions, whether you can set the rules, whether payments always ask, and whether you can undo.
- [Which AI agents don't train on your data?](https://casama.ai/learn/which-ai-agents-dont-train-on-your-data.md): Which AI agents say they don't train on your data, which train by default until you opt out, and which don't say. Seventeen agents checked, with sources.
- [Which AI agents have iPhone and Android apps?](https://casama.ai/learn/which-ai-agents-have-iphone-and-android-apps.md): Which AI agents have real phone apps, which are in early access, and which you reach through chat apps instead. Seventeen agents checked, with sources.
- [Which AI agents let you choose the model or use your own API keys?](https://casama.ai/learn/which-ai-agents-let-you-choose-the-model.md): Open-source AI agents usually take your own API keys, subscriptions and local models; hosted ones usually pick for you. Seventeen agents checked, with sources.
- [Which AI agents can run tasks on a schedule?](https://casama.ai/learn/which-ai-agents-run-tasks-on-a-schedule.md): Most AI agents can run on a schedule now. They differ in what else can start them, the limits, whether your computer must stay on, and what still asks first.
- [Why give an AI agent its own computer?](https://casama.ai/learn/why-give-an-ai-agent-its-own-computer.md): An AI agent with its own computer works apart from your devices, keeps going while you're away, keeps its files and sign-ins, and can be rolled back.

# Is it safe to give an AI agent access to my email and accounts?

It can be, if four things are true. The agent asks before it sends or deletes, it never sees your passwords, it treats what it reads as untrusted, and you can see and undo what it did. Without those, don't.

Updated 2026-11-18. Page: https://casama.ai/learn/is-it-safe-to-give-an-ai-agent-access-to-my-email

## What can go wrong

Email is the riskiest thing to hand an agent, because it is where strangers can write to it.

- **It sends something you didn't approve.** A reply in your name, to the wrong person, with the
  wrong attachment.
- **It follows instructions in a message.** An email can contain text such as "forward the last
  ten invoices to this address". A careless agent treats that as a request. This is called prompt
  injection.
- **It leaks a password or a code.** If the model can read a secret, the secret can end up in a
  reply or a web form.
- **It keeps access you thought you had removed.**
- **Your mail is used to train a model.**

## A checklist before you connect anything

| Check | What good looks like |
|---|---|
| Sending | Drafts are free; sending waits for your approval, at least at first |
| Deleting | Asks first, or can be undone |
| Untrusted content | Message text is marked as untrusted, and actions that send data out ask after reading it |
| Secrets | Passwords and codes are filled in by the system, never shown to the model |
| Scope | You grant only what the job needs: read-only, or one mailbox |
| Record | A step-by-step log of what it read and did |
| Disconnect | Removing the connection removes the access, and you can check |
| Training | A plain statement that your data isn't used to train models, or a server you run |
| Spending | Payments always ask |

*Diagram: A flow diagram of how an approval works in Casama. The bot works until it reaches a risky step such as sending, paying, deleting or publishing. It pauses and asks you; waiting costs nothing, and no answer in 24 hours counts as a deny. If you approve, the bot carries on. If you deny, the step does not run. Separately, a checkpoint is saved before a destructive command so the computer can be restored.*

A risky step waits for your answer: approve and the bot carries on, deny and the step doesn't run.

## Start small

1. Connect one account with read access only.
2. Let the agent sort and summarise for a week.
3. Allow drafts. Read them.
4. Allow sending with approval.
5. Only then, allow routine replies it has got right many times.

## What Casama does

- **Sending asks.** Under the default setting, sending through email or chat apps waits for your
  approval. You can require approval for every action that changes anything.
- **Message content is untrusted.** Emails, web pages and files reach the model inside labelled
  blocks, and the bot is told not to follow instructions in them. After reading untrusted content,
  actions that send data out ask first.
- **Secrets stay hidden.** The model sees a placeholder. Casama fills in the real value only for
  the site that secret is allowed for.
- **Per-tool rules.** For each connected app you can mark each tool read-only, makes changes, or
  always asks.
- **A record.** Every run has a timeline of its steps.
- **No training.** Your chats, memories and files aren't used to train models. If you want your
  mail to stay on your own machine, [self-host](https://casama.ai/self-hosted).

[How Casama keeps bots safe](https://casama.ai/security) covers the rest.

## Related questions

- [Which AI agents ask before they act?](https://casama.ai/learn/which-ai-agents-ask-before-they-act)
- [Self-hosted or hosted AI agent: which should I choose?](https://casama.ai/learn/self-hosted-or-hosted-ai-agent)

Join the waitlist at https://casama.ai/waitlist (Casama Cloud is invite-only for now), or run it on your own server: https://docs.casama.ai/self-hosting/

# Is OpenClaw safe, and is it free?

OpenClaw is free: MIT-licensed software from a nonprofit, with no paid tier. You pay only your AI model provider, or nothing with a local model. Whether it is safe depends on how you set it up. By its own docs, tools run on your machine with the sandbox and approval prompts off until you turn them on. With both on, on a spare machine, and with care over skills, it is far safer.

Updated 2026-11-18. Page: https://casama.ai/learn/is-openclaw-safe

## Is OpenClaw free?

Yes, entirely. OpenClaw's site says there is no subscription or paid edition, and it is run by the
OpenClaw Foundation, a nonprofit. The code is MIT-licensed.

What can cost money:

- **The AI model.** OpenClaw takes your own API keys, a ChatGPT or Claude plan, or local models.
  With a key, you pay the provider for what you use. A local model costs nothing.
- **A machine to run it on.** There is no hosted OpenClaw. It runs on your own computer or server,
  and it only answers while that machine is on.

## Is OpenClaw safe?

OpenClaw can be set up safely, but it doesn't start that way. Four facts from its own docs and from
press:

1. **Tools run on your machine.** The sandbox is optional and off by default, so the agent can
   reach what your user account can reach.
2. **Approvals are off by default.** Command approvals exist but have to be turned on.
3. **Security advisories.** The Register reported three high-impact security advisories in three
   days in February 2026, and malicious skills on its skill registry.
4. **It isn't built to keep users apart.** Its docs say a group that trusts each other can share
   one, but it isn't designed for people who don't trust each other.

None of that makes it unusable. It means OpenClaw trusts you to choose your own safety settings.

## How to run OpenClaw more safely

- **Turn on the sandbox** so tools run apart from your own files.
- **Turn on command approvals** so risky commands wait for you.
- **Use a spare machine or a virtual machine**, not the laptop with your banking and work sign-ins.
- **Read a skill before you install it.** Skills run with the agent's permissions.
- **Connect the fewest accounts you can**, and use separate logins for the agent where possible.
- **Keep it updated.** On November 18, 2026 the latest release was v2026.11.5, published the day
  before.
- **Don't share one agent** with people you wouldn't give your computer to.

## Who OpenClaw suits

OpenClaw is a strong choice if you are comfortable with a terminal, want the most chat apps (about
29), want software with no paid tier at all, and will set up the sandbox and approvals yourself. It
has the largest community of the agents we track, with about 395,000 GitHub stars.

## If you'd rather not set it up yourself

Some agents start with these protections on. Casama gives each bot its own sandboxed Linux
computer, asks before risky steps by default, always asks before payments, and saves a checkpoint
before destructive commands. It is free to self-host and has a free hosted plan. It is also much
newer than OpenClaw, with a small community and fewer chat apps.

Compare them side by side in [Casama vs OpenClaw](https://casama.ai/alternatives/openclaw), or see eight
[OpenClaw alternatives](https://casama.ai/compare/openclaw-alternatives).

## Questions

### Does OpenClaw have a paid plan?

No. There is no subscription or paid edition, and no hosted version.

### Can OpenClaw access my files?

By default, tools run on your machine with the sandbox off, so it can reach what your user account
can. Turn on the sandbox to limit that.

### Does OpenClaw train on my data?

There is no OpenClaw cloud, so OpenClaw itself doesn't receive your data. Your model provider's
policy applies, unless you use a local model. See
[which AI agents don't train on your data](https://casama.ai/learn/which-ai-agents-dont-train-on-your-data).

### Are OpenClaw skills safe?

Treat each one like software from a stranger. Malicious skills were reported on its registry in
February 2026. Read what a skill does before installing it.

## Related questions

- [Is it safe to give an AI agent access to my email and accounts?](https://casama.ai/learn/is-it-safe-to-give-an-ai-agent-access-to-my-email)
- [Which AI agents ask before they act?](https://casama.ai/learn/which-ai-agents-ask-before-they-act)

# How do I run AI agents on my own server from my phone?

Run the agent software on a computer you own, give that computer an address your phone can reach, and sign in from a phone app. The hard part used to be the address. A relay now does it with no domain, port forwarding or VPN.

Updated 2026-11-18. Page: https://casama.ai/learn/run-ai-agents-on-your-own-server-from-your-phone

## Why it's awkward

A server on your laptop or in a cupboard at home sits behind your router. Your phone, out on a
mobile network, can't reach it. The usual fixes all have a catch:

| Way | Catch |
|---|---|
| Port forwarding and a domain | You open your home network to the internet and manage certificates |
| A VPN to your home network | Every phone needs a VPN app that is switched on |
| A VPS instead of a home server | Monthly cost, and your data is no longer at home |
| A tunnel service | Extra setup, and another company in the path |

And reaching the server is only half of it. A real phone app also needs push notifications, which
only work through Apple's and Google's services, tied to the app in the store.

## What you need for it to feel like a normal app

1. **An address** that works from any network, over HTTPS.
2. **A native app** on the phone that can sign in to your server, not only a web page.
3. **Notifications** that arrive when a bot needs you or finishes.
4. **An easy sign-in**, since typing a long address and a password on a phone is no fun.
5. **Your data staying home.** Traffic should pass through to your machine, not be stored along
   the way.

## How Casama does it

Casama is an open-source AI agent app you can run on your own computer for free. Its relay is
called Casama Link.

1. **Run the server.** One command with Docker, or choose **Run Casama on This Computer** in the
   Mac or Linux app.
2. **Turn on Casama Link.** Choose **Use on Your Phone** in the desktop app's settings, or run
   `casama selfhost remote on`. Your server gets its own `casama.link` address. Nothing to set up
   on your router.
3. **Scan the code.** Open the Casama app from the App Store or Google Play and scan the QR code
   on your computer's screen. You're signed in.
4. **Get notifications.** Approvals and finished tasks reach your phone like any other app's.

Your bots, chats, memory and files stay on your server. Casama's side keeps a record of the linked
server (its name, its address and when it last checked in) and passes notifications along.

## What it costs

Remote access through Casama Link is free on every plan, including for self-hosted servers.
Watching a bot's computer live while you're away from home comes with Plus and up.

## Good to know

- **The computer must be on.** A laptop that sleeps takes your bots with it. A small always-on
  machine, or a VPS, avoids that.
- **Bot computers are the heavy part.** If your machine is small, Casama Link can also let Casama
  Cloud run the bots' computers while everything else stays on your server.
- **You can use your own domain instead.** Casama Link is optional. With your own domain you can
  still link the server so notifications reach the store apps.

The [remote access guide](https://docs.casama.ai/self-hosting/remote-access) has every step.

## Related questions

- [How do I self-host an AI agent?](https://casama.ai/learn/how-to-self-host-an-ai-agent)
- [Self-hosted or hosted AI agent: which should I choose?](https://casama.ai/learn/self-hosted-or-hosted-ai-agent)
- [Which AI agents have iPhone and Android apps?](https://casama.ai/learn/which-ai-agents-have-iphone-and-android-apps)

Join the waitlist at https://casama.ai/waitlist (Casama Cloud is invite-only for now), or run it on your own server: https://docs.casama.ai/self-hosting/

# Self-hosted or hosted AI agent: which should you choose?

Host it yourself if you want your data on your own machine, any model you like, and no monthly fee. Use a hosted agent if you want to start in a minute and never think about servers. Some products let you do either, or both.

Updated 2026-11-18. Page: https://casama.ai/learn/self-hosted-or-hosted-ai-agent

## The trade-offs

| | Self-hosted | Hosted |
|---|---|---|
| Setup | An hour or less, and a machine with Docker | Sign up |
| Upkeep | You update and back up | The vendor does |
| Where your data lives | Your machine | The vendor's servers |
| Models | Any provider, or local models | Whatever the vendor offers |
| What you pay | Your hardware, plus model providers directly | A subscription, often with usage on top |
| Limits | Your hardware | The plan's limits |
| If the vendor changes or closes | Your copy keeps running | You move |
| Reach from your phone | Needs a public address or a relay | Built in |
| Region locks | None | Sometimes |

*Diagram: Two columns comparing Casama Cloud with self-hosted Casama. Casama Cloud: Casama runs the servers and computers, Casama picks and runs the models, you pay with credits, and you just sign up and start. Self-hosted: your own server or Mac runs everything, you use your own model keys or local models, it is free to run, and you update and back up yourself.*

Casama Cloud is run for you and paid in credits; self-hosted is free to run on your own machine with your own models.

## Choose self-hosted if

- Your email, files or customer data shouldn't sit on someone else's servers.
- You want a specific model, your own keys, or a local model so nothing leaves your network.
- You already run a home server or a VPS and Docker doesn't worry you.
- You want many users or many bots without paying per seat.
- You want to read, change or extend the software.

## Choose hosted if

- You want to try it today.
- Nobody on your team wants to look after a server.
- You'd rather pay a known monthly price than manage model keys and bills.
- You need it to be there when your own machine is off.

## The usual worries about self-hosting

**"I can't reach a home server from my phone."** That used to need a domain, port forwarding or a
VPN. A relay service can give your server a public address instead.

**"Bots need computers to work on, and that's heavy."** It is the heaviest part. Some products let
a self-hosted server borrow cloud computers for its bots and keep everything else at home.

**"I'll forget to update it."** Pick software with a one-command update, and put it in your
calendar.

**"Local models aren't good enough."** For long, tool-heavy tasks the best hosted models are still
ahead. Many people run a local model for private or simple work and a hosted one for the rest.

## You don't have to pick one

With Casama you can do either or mix them:

- **Self-hosted** is free: one command installs the whole stack with Docker on a VPS, a home
  server or a laptop, with no limit on users or bots. Use any provider, your ChatGPT plan or local
  models.
- **Casama Cloud** has a free plan and paid plans from $15 a month with credits included.
- **Casama Link** gives a self-hosted server an address your phone can reach, free, with no
  domain or port forwarding. It can also let Casama Cloud run the bot computers and model calls
  for your server, while your chats, memory and files stay with you.

The apps are the same either way, and a workspace exports in full, so you can change your mind.

## Related questions

- [How do I self-host an AI agent?](https://casama.ai/learn/how-to-self-host-an-ai-agent)
- [Can AI agents run on my own models?](https://casama.ai/learn/can-ai-agents-run-on-local-models)

Join the waitlist at https://casama.ai/waitlist (Casama Cloud is invite-only for now), or run it on your own server: https://docs.casama.ai/self-hosting/

# What is a computer use agent, and which ones let you take over?

A computer use agent is an AI agent that operates a computer the way a person does. It looks at the screen, clicks, types, opens a browser and runs programs, instead of only calling apps through their APIs. That lets it use any website or app, including ones with no integration. The big questions are whose computer it uses, and whether you can watch it and take over.

Updated 2026-11-18. Page: https://casama.ai/learn/what-is-a-computer-use-agent

## How it works

The agent runs in a loop. It takes a screenshot or reads the page, asks an AI model what to do
next, then clicks, types or runs a command. It checks the result and goes again until the task is
done or it needs you. See [how AI agents work](https://casama.ai/learn/how-do-ai-agents-work).

Many agents mix the two styles: an API when an app has one, and the screen when it doesn't, such
as a supplier's web form or an old booking site.

## Whose computer?

| Where it works | Upside | Downside |
|---|---|---|
| **Your own computer** | Your files and sign-ins are already there | It can reach everything you can, and it stops when you shut the lid |
| **A computer of its own** | A mistake stays on that machine, and it keeps working when you're away | You sign in to sites for it, once |

The first is quicker to set up. The second is safer to leave running. See
[why give an AI agent its own computer](https://casama.ai/learn/why-give-an-ai-agent-its-own-computer).

## Which agents let you watch and take over

| Agent | Its computer | Watch or take over |
|---|---|---|
| **Casama** | Each bot has its own sandboxed Linux computer | Watch live and take over |
| **Meta Muse** | One cloud computer per person | Watch and take over |
| **ChatGPT Dots** | Each dot has its own cloud computer | You can open it |
| **Claude Cowork and Duet** | Cowork: cloud sessions. Duet: its own cloud computer | Cowork you can watch; Duet you can't watch or take over |
| **Hark Pro** | Its own cloud browser per person | You can watch it |
| **Agent Zero** | A Docker container with its own Linux desktop, terminal and browser | A desktop you can watch |
| **Manus** | A cloud sandbox with a browser, per person | Not covered in the sources we checked |
| **Grok Bot** | One cloud computer per person, shared by all of that person's Bots | Not covered in the sources we checked |
| **Rakazo** | Each bot has its own container or cloud computer | Not covered in the sources we checked |
| **OpenClaw, Hermes Agent, nanobot** | Your machine by default | It's your own screen |

Checked on November 18, 2026; the sources are at the end. We make Casama.

## Why taking over matters

- **Sign-ins.** A site asks for a password or a two-step code. You type it yourself, and the agent
  carries on.
- **Stuck steps.** A pop-up or an odd layout confuses it. You click past it in seconds.
- **Trust.** Watching an agent work for a week is how most people decide what to let it do alone.

An agent you can only read about after the fact is harder to correct and harder to trust.

## Computer use in Casama

Each bot has its own sandboxed Linux computer with a shell, files and a browser that stays signed
in. A desktop computer adds a real screen you can watch live in the Casama app and control at any
time. When a site needs you, the bot asks you to take over: you sign in yourself in the live view,
and nothing you type reaches the bot.

The bot can't reach your devices or files you didn't share. Before a command that deletes data, a
checkpoint of its computer is saved. You can also lend a bot your own machine when it needs
something only you have. See the [computers guide](https://docs.casama.ai/guide/computers).

## Questions

### Is a computer use agent the same as browser automation?

No. Browser automation follows a script you wrote. A computer use agent decides each step itself,
so it copes with pages it hasn't seen, and it can make mistakes a script wouldn't.

### Is it safe to let an AI agent use a computer?

Safer on a computer of its own, with approvals before risky steps and a way to undo. See
[which AI agents ask before they act](https://casama.ai/learn/which-ai-agents-ask-before-they-act).

### Can a computer use agent work while I'm away?

Yes, if its computer is in the cloud or on an always-on server. An agent on your laptop stops when
the laptop sleeps.

## Related questions

- [Why give an AI agent its own computer?](https://casama.ai/learn/why-give-an-ai-agent-its-own-computer)
- [What is an AI agent?](https://casama.ai/learn/what-is-an-ai-agent)

# What is an AI agent?

An AI agent is software that uses an AI model to carry out a task for you, step by step, using tools such as a browser, files and your apps. A chatbot tells you how to do something. An agent does it and reports back.

Updated 2026-11-18. Page: https://casama.ai/learn/what-is-an-ai-agent

## The short version

Give a chatbot the request "book a table for four on Friday" and it writes you a list of
restaurants. Give an agent the same request and it opens the booking site, picks a time, fills in
the form, asks you before confirming, and tells you when it is done.

Three things make that possible:

1. **A model that plans.** The AI model decides what to do next, looks at the result, and decides
   again. This loop repeats until the task is done.
2. **Tools.** The agent can do things, not only write: open web pages, run commands, read and
   write files, send messages, use the apps you connect.
3. **A place to work.** It needs somewhere to run those tools: your own computer, a browser, or a
   computer of its own in the cloud.

*Diagram: A diagram of how an AI agent works. A goal enters a loop of three stages: plan, which picks one step; act, which uses tools on the agent's computer; and check, which reads the result. If the task is not done, the loop goes round again from plan. The agent leaves the loop in one of two ways: done, when the task is finished, or ask you, when it needs a decision or approval.*

An agent plans a step, acts with its tools, checks the result and repeats until it is done or needs you.

## What an agent can do

- **Work that takes many steps**: research a topic across twenty sources and write it up, or clean
  a spreadsheet and chart it.
- **Work in your apps**: sort an inbox, draft replies, move meetings, update a ticket.
- **Work that repeats**: a morning brief, a weekly report, a price check every hour.
- **Work while you're away**: an agent with its own computer keeps going after you close the chat.

## What to look for in one

| Question | Why it matters |
|---|---|
| Where does it run? | On your machine it can touch your files. On a separate computer, mistakes stay there. |
| Does it ask first? | Sending, paying and deleting should wait for your OK. |
| Does it remember? | Without memory you explain your preferences every time. |
| Can it start by itself? | Schedules and triggers turn a helper into a teammate. |
| What does it cost? | Each step uses a model, so long tasks cost more. Look for budgets. |
| Who can see your data? | Check whether it trains on your data, and whether you can run it yourself. |

## Where agents go wrong

Agents make mistakes that chatbots can't, because they act. A model can misread a page, repeat a
failing step, or follow instructions hidden in a web page it was only meant to read. Good agent
software limits the damage: a sandboxed computer, approvals for risky steps, spending limits, and a
way to undo.

## How Casama fits

Casama is an open-source app for AI agents it calls teammates, or bots. Each bot has its own
sandboxed Linux computer, a memory you can read and edit, and rules for what it must ask before
doing. Bots run on schedules and triggers, and you reach them from apps on every platform. You can
[run it on your own server](https://casama.ai/self-hosted) for free or use Casama Cloud.

## Related questions

- [AI agent vs chatbot: what's the difference?](https://casama.ai/learn/ai-agent-vs-chatbot)

- [Is it safe to give an AI agent access to my email?](https://casama.ai/learn/is-it-safe-to-give-an-ai-agent-access-to-my-email)

# What is an AI employee?

An AI employee is an AI agent given a standing job. It has a role, the tools for that role, a memory, a schedule and limits on what it may do alone. "AI worker", "AI intern", "AI coworker" and "digital employee" are names for the same idea. It is software, so it doesn't replace a person's judgement, but it can take over work that is repeatable and checkable.

Updated 2026-11-18. Page: https://casama.ai/learn/what-is-an-ai-employee

## What makes it an "employee" and not a chatbot

| | Chatbot | AI employee |
|---|---|---|
| Job | Whatever you type | One standing role |
| Starts work | When you ask | On a schedule, or when something arrives |
| Tools | Few or none | The apps and files the role needs |
| Memory | This conversation | Your preferences, your customers, past work |
| Place to work | The chat box | A computer: yours, or one of its own |
| Supervision | You read every reply | You approve the risky steps and review the rest |

## Jobs that suit one

Work is a good fit when it repeats, has a clear "done", and can be checked afterwards:

- **Support**: answer common questions from your help documents; pass on the rest.
- **Inbox and calendar**: sort, draft, propose times, chase replies.
- **Research**: a weekly price or competitor check with sources.
- **Admin**: forms, data entry, matching receipts, chasing invoices.
- **Reporting**: a Monday summary pulled from several tools.
- **Coding chores**: run a coding agent on a failing test and report back.

## Jobs that don't

- Anything where a wrong answer is costly and hard to notice: legal advice, medical decisions,
  final sign-off on money.
- Work that depends on relationships or taste.
- One-off tasks that take longer to explain than to do.

## What "hiring" one involves

1. **Write the job down.** One role per AI employee. "Answer support email from the help docs, and
   never promise a refund" beats "help with customers".
2. **Give it the tools for that job only.** The support bot doesn't need your bank.
3. **Decide what it must ask.** Sending, paying and deleting should wait for a person at first.
4. **Set a budget.** Per task and per day, so a confused run can't spend much.
5. **Review for a week.** Read what it did, correct it, and let it remember the corrections.
6. **Loosen slowly.** Allow the actions it has got right many times.

## What it costs

There is no salary, but each step uses an AI model, and a computer costs something to run.
A typical short task costs cents. A long research task can cost a dollar or more. Compare prices by
what is included: model usage, computer hours, seats, and what happens when you go over.

## Where they go wrong

- **Confidently wrong.** A model can state something false. Sources and a record of each step let
  you check.
- **Tricked by content.** An email or web page can contain instructions. Good software treats that
  content as untrusted and asks before sending data out.
- **Stuck in a loop.** Limits on repeated failures and on spending stop a run that isn't getting
  anywhere.
- **Over-trusted.** The failures that hurt come from giving broad access on day one.

## AI employees in Casama

Casama calls them bots. Each bot has instructions, a model, memory, skills and its own sandboxed
Linux computer. Built-in personas give you a starting point for common jobs: Assistant, Support,
Sales, Ops, Researcher, Inbox triage, Coder and others. Bots run on schedules and triggers, work in
group chats with your team, and stop for approval before risky steps. Each has a budget per run and
per day. See [AI agents for small business](https://casama.ai/use-cases/ai-agents-for-small-business).

## Related questions

- [What is an AI teammate?](https://casama.ai/learn/what-is-an-ai-teammate)
- [Which AI agents ask before they act?](https://casama.ai/learn/which-ai-agents-ask-before-they-act)

Join the waitlist at https://casama.ai/waitlist (Casama Cloud is invite-only for now), or run it on your own server: https://docs.casama.ai/self-hosting/

# What is an AI teammate?

An AI teammate is an AI agent that stays. It has a role, remembers how you work, starts tasks without being asked, and works alongside people in the same chats. An agent finishes a task. A teammate holds a job.

Updated 2026-11-18. Page: https://casama.ai/learn/what-is-an-ai-teammate

## From agent to teammate

"AI agent" describes how the software works: a model that uses tools in a loop. "AI teammate"
describes how you work with it. The difference is what carries over from one task to the next:

| | One-off AI agent | AI teammate |
|---|---|---|
| Lifetime | One task, then gone | Stays for months |
| Role | Whatever you ask this time | A standing job: assistant, researcher, support |
| Memory | Starts fresh | Remembers preferences, people and past work |
| Initiative | Waits for a request | Runs on schedules, reacts to events, suggests work |
| Workspace | Borrowed for the task | Its own computer, with its files where it left them |
| Working with people | One person, one chat | Group chats, shared spaces, handing work to others |

## What makes one useful

- **A clear job.** "Research" or "customer support" works better than "everything".
- **Memory you can check.** A teammate that remembers the wrong thing needs correcting, so you
  should be able to read and edit what it knows.
- **Somewhere to keep its work.** Files, sign-ins and half-finished tasks should still be there
  tomorrow.
- **Ways to reach you.** A phone notification, a chat app, an email: wherever you already are.
- **Limits.** What it may do alone, what it must ask about, and how much it may spend.

## A day with an AI teammate

A personal assistant bot might:

1. Send a morning brief at 7:30 with today's meetings and the three emails that need you.
2. Notice a meeting clash and suggest a new time, with a button to do it.
3. Draft replies to routine emails and wait for your approval before sending.
4. Book the dinner you mentioned yesterday, because it remembered the restaurant you like.
5. Write up what it did, with the cost.

None of that needed a prompt after the first week.

## Who offers AI teammates

Several products now use the idea: hosted ones from the large AI labs, and open-source ones you can
run yourself. They differ most in where the teammate works (its own computer or yours), what it
asks before doing, which models it can use, and whether you can host it. Our
[comparison pages](https://casama.ai/alternatives/) put them side by side.

## AI teammates in Casama

Casama calls its teammates bots. Each one has instructions, a model, memory, skills, its own
sandboxed Linux computer and limits you set. Bots send check-ins and suggestions, run routines on
schedules and triggers, work in group chats with people and other bots, and reach you in the app,
by push notification or in chat apps such as Slack and Telegram.

## Related questions

- [What is an AI agent?](https://casama.ai/learn/what-is-an-ai-agent)
- [Why give an AI agent its own computer?](https://casama.ai/learn/why-give-an-ai-agent-its-own-computer)

Join the waitlist at https://casama.ai/waitlist (Casama Cloud is invite-only for now), or run it on your own server: https://docs.casama.ai/self-hosting/

# What is MCP, and what is an MCP client?

MCP, the Model Context Protocol, is a standard way for an AI app to use tools and data from somewhere else. An MCP server offers the tools. An MCP client is the AI app that connects and uses them.

Updated 2026-11-18. Page: https://casama.ai/learn/what-is-mcp

## The idea

Before MCP, every AI app needed its own connector for every service: one for the calendar, one for
the database, one for the ticket tracker, written again for each app. MCP is one plug shape. A
service publishes an MCP server once, and any AI app that speaks MCP can use it.

| Word | Meaning | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| MCP server | A program that offers tools, data or prompts | A server for GitHub, a database, your notes, a company's own system |
| MCP client | The AI app that connects to servers and lets its model use their tools | Chat apps, coding assistants, agent platforms |
| Tool | One thing a server can do | "Search issues", "run a query", "create a page" |

A server can run on your own computer or on the internet. Remote servers usually ask you to sign
in, so the AI app acts with your permissions and not more.

## What it means for AI agents

An agent is only as useful as the things it can reach. MCP widens that without waiting for the
agent's maker to build each connection:

- **More tools.** If a service has an MCP server, your agent can use it.
- **Your own tools.** A small MCP server in front of an internal system gives an agent a safe,
  narrow way in.
- **Both directions.** An agent platform can be a client (its agents use other servers) and a
  server (other AI apps hand work to its agents).

## What to check before connecting one

- **Who runs the server.** A tool is code that acts with your access. Use servers from the service
  itself or a source you trust.
- **What each tool can do.** Reading is different from deleting. Good clients let you set which
  tools need approval.
- **What the tool's output can say.** Results come from outside, so they should be treated as
  untrusted, like a web page.

## MCP in Casama

Casama works in both directions.

**As a client.** A bot can use tools from MCP servers you add, next to its built-in tools and
connected apps. Each tool gets a risk level you can change (read-only, makes changes, always
asks), so approvals apply to MCP tools the same way as to everything else.

**As a server.** Casama has its own MCP server, so AI apps such as Claude, ChatGPT or a coding
assistant can talk to your bots and hand them work. The
[MCP guide](https://docs.casama.ai/guide/mcp) shows how to connect.

**For builders.** Casama's documentation is also available over MCP with no sign-in, at
`https://api.casama.ai/mcp/docs`, so a coding agent can look up the API while it works.
`npx -y @casama/mcp` adds a gallery search.

## Questions

### Is MCP only for developers?

No. Adding a server is usually pasting an address and signing in. Building one takes code.

### Is MCP the same as an API?

An API is how programs talk to a service. MCP is a layer on top that describes tools in a way an
AI model can choose from and call.

### Do I need MCP to use an AI agent?

No. It is one way to give an agent more tools.

## Related questions

- [What is an AI agent?](https://casama.ai/learn/what-is-an-ai-agent)
- [How do AI agents work?](https://casama.ai/learn/how-do-ai-agents-work)

# Which AI agents ask before they act?

Most AI agents ask before some actions. What differs is which actions, whether you can set the rules yourself, whether payments always ask, and whether a mistake can be undone. Here is how to tell a real approval system from a single on-off switch.

Updated 2026-11-18. Page: https://casama.ai/learn/which-ai-agents-ask-before-they-act

## What "asks before acting" should mean

An approval is only useful if it stops the right things and nothing else. An agent that asks about
everything gets ignored, and one that asks about nothing gets switched off after its first mistake.

A good system has five parts:

1. **Risk per action.** Reading a page is not sending an email. Each kind of action should have its
   own level.
2. **Your rules.** You should be able to say "always allow this", "always ask about that", per
   agent and per app.
3. **Hard stops.** Some actions, such as paying, should ask whatever you set.
4. **A clear request.** The approval should show exactly what will happen: the recipient, the
   amount, the file.
5. **A way back.** A snapshot before destructive steps, so "approve" isn't the last line of
   defence.

## Questions to ask of any agent

| Question | Why |
|---|---|
| Can I choose what needs approval, or is it one switch? | One switch means all or nothing |
| Do payments always ask? | A setting you forgot shouldn't spend money |
| Where do approvals reach me? | If only in a browser tab, work stalls when you're away |
| Does a waiting task cost money? | Some bill for idle time |
| What happens after it reads a suspicious page? | It should get more careful, not carry on |
| Can I undo an approved step? | Checkpoints matter most when you approved by mistake |
| Is the rule set written down? | Published rules can be checked. "We're careful" can't |

## How to compare products

Vendors describe approvals in very different words, and the details change often. Rather than
trust a summary, look for each product's own page on permissions or safety, and check it against
the table above. Our [comparison pages](https://casama.ai/alternatives/) record what each product says publicly,
with the source and the date we read it.

## How approvals work in Casama

Every tool has a risk level, and each bot has one of three settings:

| Setting | The bot asks before |
|---|---|
| Ask before acting | Every action that changes something |
| Ask for risky actions (the default) | Sending email or chat messages, calling people, making a page public, deleting outside its workspace, paid data lookups, and tools you marked "always asks" |
| Act on its own | Nothing, except high-risk actions on your own computer |

*Diagram: A flow diagram of how an approval works in Casama. The bot works until it reaches a risky step such as sending, paying, deleting or publishing. It pauses and asks you; waiting costs nothing, and no answer in 24 hours counts as a deny. If you approve, the bot carries on. If you deny, the step does not run. Separately, a checkpoint is saved before a destructive command so the computer can be restored.*

A risky step waits for your answer: approve and the bot carries on, deny and the step doesn't run.

On top of that:

- **Payments always ask**, under every setting.
- **Action rules** let you allow, limit or always ask about a specific tool for a specific bot.
- **Approvals reach you** in the chat, in a "Needs you" list, by push notification, and in Slack
  as buttons.
- **After reading untrusted content**, actions that send data out ask first.
- **A waiting run costs nothing** and survives a server restart. A request with no answer after 24
  hours counts as denied.
- **Checkpoints** are saved before destructive commands.

The full rules are in the [autonomy guide](https://docs.casama.ai/guide/autonomy).

# Which AI agents don't train on your data?

Casama, Hark Pro, Lindy and n8n say they don't use your data to train AI models, and Manus says so for team plans. Instinct, Meta Muse and Claude's consumer plans train by default until you switch it off. Self-hosted agents have no cloud of their own, so your model provider's policy applies. Several products don't say either way.

Updated 2026-11-18. Page: https://casama.ai/learn/which-ai-agents-dont-train-on-your-data

## The list

| Agent | Training on your data |
|---|---|
| **Casama** | Not used to train models |
| **Hark Pro** | Says it doesn't train on your data |
| **Lindy** | No, says Lindy |
| **n8n** | Says assistant data isn't used to train AI providers' models |
| **Manus** | Team plans say no; individual plans are unclear |
| **Grok Bot** | A training opt-out exists |
| **Instinct** | On by default; you can opt out |
| **Meta Muse** | On by default; you can turn it off |
| **Claude Cowork and Duet** | On for consumer plans unless you switch it off |
| **OpenClaw** | There is no OpenClaw cloud; your model provider's policy applies |
| **Hermes Agent** | With your own keys only your provider sees your data; Nous Portal may train on prompts unless Privacy Mode is on |
| **NanoClaw** | Not stated; self-hosted data stays on your machine |
| **Agent Zero** | Not stated; it runs on your machine and sends prompts to the model you choose |
| **nanobot** | Not stated |
| **Rakazo** | Not stated either way |
| **MausBot** | Not stated |
| **OpenBot** | Not stated for OpenBot |

Checked on November 18, 2026, from each product's privacy pages and terms; the sources are at the
end. We didn't find a statement for ChatGPT Dots. We make Casama.

## Two layers to check

An agent usually has two companies behind it: the one that makes the agent, and the one that runs
the AI model. Both see your requests.

1. **The agent maker.** Do they use your chats, files and memories to train anything? Is that on
   by default? Is the answer the same on free and paid plans?
2. **The model provider.** When the agent sends a step to a model, that provider's terms apply.
   With your own API key you choose the provider and can read its terms. With a hosted agent, ask
   which providers it uses.

A local model removes the second layer: nothing leaves your machine.

## Training isn't the only question

A product can promise no training and still keep your data longer than you'd like. Also check:

- **Who can see it.** Meta says it can technically access a Muse agent's computer today; its
  stronger private mode hasn't shipped.
- **Where it is stored.** Lindy's privacy notice doesn't say which region holds your data.
- **Whether you can export and delete it**, and how long deleted data lingers.
- **What the agent can reach.** An agent that works on your own computer can read whatever you can.

## Your data in Casama

- Your chats, memories and files are used to run Casama for you and for nothing else. They are not
  used to train AI models, sold, or used for ads.
- You can export everything, delete your account, set how long run history is kept, and turn on
  encryption for a workspace's content.
- Secrets never reach the AI model: a bot uses a placeholder, and the real value is filled in only
  for the site it's allowed for.
- On Casama Cloud, requests go to the AI models Casama runs your bots on. If you want nothing to
  leave your own machine, [self-host Casama](https://casama.ai/self-hosted) with a local model through Ollama.

See [how Casama keeps your data safe](https://casama.ai/security).

## Questions

### What is the most private AI assistant?

One you run yourself on a local model: nothing leaves your machine. Among hosted ones, start with
those that say they don't train on your data, then check who can access it and where it is stored.

### Does a training opt-out cover what I already sent?

It depends on the product. Its terms should say whether switching training off covers what you
already sent or only new conversations. If they don't say, ask before you rely on it.

### Do open-source AI agents train on my data?

The agent software itself usually has no cloud to send data to. Your model provider's terms decide
what happens to your prompts, unless you use a local model.

# Which AI agents have iPhone and Android apps?

Of the AI agents we track, OpenClaw, Rakazo, Grok Bot, Claude, ChatGPT, Meta Muse, Hark Pro and Casama list apps for both iPhone and Android. Manus lists an iPhone app. OpenBot's and MausBot's phone apps aren't generally available. Most of the rest have no phone app, and you reach them through a chat app such as Telegram or WhatsApp.

Updated 2026-11-18. Page: https://casama.ai/learn/which-ai-agents-have-iphone-and-android-apps

## The list

| Agent | Phone apps | Other ways in |
|---|---|---|
| **Casama** | iPhone, iPad and Android | Mac, Windows, Linux, web, and ten chat apps |
| **OpenClaw** | iPhone and Android | Mac, Windows, Linux, and about 29 chat apps; no hosted web app |
| **Rakazo** | iPhone, iPad and Android | Web, Mac, Windows, Linux |
| **Grok Bot** | iPhone, iPad and Android | Mac, Windows, Linux, X, Slack, Teams |
| **Claude Cowork and Duet** | iPhone and Android | Mac, Windows, Linux (beta), web |
| **ChatGPT Dots** | The ChatGPT phone app | ChatGPT on desktop and web, Slack, Teams |
| **Meta Muse** | iPhone and Android | Web, WhatsApp; US only |
| **Hark Pro** | iPhone, iPad and Android | Web |
| **Manus** | iPhone and iPad are listed | Web, Mac (Apple silicon), Windows, Slack, email |
| **OpenBot** | Early access | Mac and Windows; Slack and Teams in early access |
| **MausBot** | Handed out through Discord, not in the stores | Mac, Windows, Linux (beta) |
| **Hermes Agent** | None yet | Mac and Windows apps, a terminal app, more than 20 chat apps |
| **Agent Zero** | None | A launcher for Windows, Mac and Linux, a web app, Telegram, WhatsApp, email |
| **nanobot** | None; its web app works on phones | Terminal, many chat apps |
| **NanoClaw** | None | Chat apps and a terminal |
| **Lindy** | None listed | Web app, a Chrome extension, Slack, iMessage and SMS, email |
| **Instinct** | None needed | Text message and phone call |

Checked on November 18, 2026, from each product's own pages; the sources are at the end. We make
Casama.

## Does it matter if the agent has no phone app?

Less than you might think, for talking to it. Most agents that run on your own machine reach you
through a chat app you already have, and a message in Telegram or WhatsApp works anywhere.

A phone app matters for three other things:

1. **Approvals.** If the agent asks before risky steps, you want to answer from your lock screen,
   not find a laptop. A push notification with Approve and Deny is faster than a chat reply.
2. **Watching its screen.** Agents with a computer of their own can show it live. That needs an
   app, or at least a phone-sized web page.
3. **Your own server.** A self-hosted agent sits on your network. A phone app that can reach it
   from outside, without you opening ports, is hard to replace with a chat app.

## What to check in any phone app

| Question | Why |
|---|---|
| Is it in the App Store and Google Play? | Apps handed out by link or by invite are harder to keep updated |
| Can I approve or deny from a notification? | Otherwise work waits until you open the app |
| Can I watch or take over the agent's computer? | You'll want to when a site needs a sign-in |
| Does it work with my own server? | Some apps only talk to the vendor's cloud |
| Is it the full product or a remote control? | Some phone apps only chat; settings live on the desktop |

## Casama's apps

Casama has native apps for iPhone, iPad, Android, Mac, Windows and Linux, and a web app. The same
apps work with Casama Cloud and with a server you run yourself. On a self-hosted server, Casama
Link gives it an address your phone can reach from anywhere, free on every plan.

From the phone app you can chat with each bot, approve or deny from a push notification, watch a
bot's computer live and take over, and see what each run cost. See
[run AI agents on your own server from your phone](https://casama.ai/learn/run-ai-agents-on-your-own-server-from-your-phone).

Honest limits: Casama is new, first released in November 2026, and reaches ten chat apps, fewer
than OpenClaw's 29 or so.

## Questions

### Which open-source AI agents have phone apps?

OpenClaw, Rakazo and Casama list apps for both iPhone and Android. Hermes Agent, Agent Zero,
NanoClaw and nanobot don't have one; you reach them through chat apps or a web page.

### What is the best AI assistant app for iPhone?

For an assistant that acts, not just answers, look at what it can do from the phone: approvals,
watching its screen, and reaching it when you're away. Our list of the
[best AI personal assistants](https://casama.ai/compare/best-ai-personal-assistants) compares eight.

### Can I use an AI agent from my phone without a phone app?

Yes. Many agents connect to Telegram, WhatsApp, Signal, iMessage or SMS, and you message them like
a person. Instinct is built around texts and calls alone.

# Which AI agents let you choose the model or use your own API keys?

Almost every open-source AI agent lets you choose the model: your own API key, a subscription you already pay for, or a local model. Almost every hosted one picks the model for you. Casama does both: on your own server you choose any provider or a local model, and on Casama Cloud, Casama picks.

Updated 2026-11-18. Page: https://casama.ai/learn/which-ai-agents-let-you-choose-the-model

## Three ways to bring a model

1. **Your own API key.** You pay the provider, such as Anthropic, OpenAI or Google, for what you
   use, with nothing added in between.
2. **A subscription you already have.** Some agents sign in with a ChatGPT, Claude or other plan,
   so there is no new bill, within that plan's limits.
3. **A local model.** Run one with Ollama or a similar tool on your own hardware. Nothing is billed
   and nothing leaves the machine, but local models are weaker on long tasks.

## The list

| Agent | Choice of model |
|---|---|
| **Casama** | Self-hosted: any provider, a ChatGPT plan, or local models. Cloud: Casama picks |
| **OpenClaw** | Your own keys, a ChatGPT or Claude plan, or local models |
| **Hermes Agent** | Your own keys, Nous Portal, some subscriptions, or local models |
| **Rakazo** | Your own keys, a ChatGPT plan, local models, or Rakazo credits at the provider's price |
| **Agent Zero** | Your own keys, a ChatGPT sign-in, or local models through Ollama or LM Studio |
| **nanobot** | Your own keys, Codex, Copilot or Grok sign-in, or local models; fallbacks supported |
| **NanoClaw** | Claude by default, with a key or subscription; Codex, Cursor and OpenCode as options |
| **MausBot** | None included: it drives AI tools you're already signed in to, or API keys |
| **OpenBot** | Your own keys or subscriptions, or any OpenAI-style endpoint |
| **n8n** | Many providers with your own keys, or local models through Ollama |
| **Lindy** | Lindy picks per task; you can choose per task |
| **Claude Cowork and Duet** | Claude models only |
| **ChatGPT Dots** | OpenAI's model; no choice |
| **Manus** | Manus picks; no choice on standard plans |
| **Grok Bot** | No choice, and you aren't shown which model ran |
| **Meta Muse** | Meta's Muse Spark model only |
| **Hark Pro** | Hark chooses; no choice |

Checked on November 18, 2026, from each product's own pages; the sources are at the end. Instinct
doesn't say which model it uses. We make Casama.

## Why it matters

- **Cost.** With your own key you pay the provider's price and can send easy work to a cheaper
  model. With a subscription, an agent can be no extra cost at all.
- **Quality.** The best model for writing code isn't always the best for reading a long contract.
  Choosing lets you match the model to the job.
- **Privacy.** With your own key, your provider's data policy applies, and you can pick a provider
  whose terms you've read. A local model keeps everything on your machine.
- **Lock-in.** An agent tied to one model maker moves only as fast as that maker does.

## The trade-off

Choosing a model means setting it up: a key to create, a bill to watch, a local server to keep
running. Hosted agents that pick for you skip all of that. If you don't want to think about models,
a hosted plan is fine. If you do, an agent that takes your own key is worth the setup.

## Models in Casama

On a self-hosted server you add keys for Anthropic, OpenAI, Google Gemini, xAI or OpenRouter, sign
in with a ChatGPT plan, or point Casama at local models through Ollama. You pay providers directly,
and local model calls are recorded at $0. Each bot has its own model, with fallbacks if one is unavailable.

On Casama Cloud, Casama picks the models, so there are no keys to add, and you pay in credits, where a
credit is a dollar. You can't bring your own key there. If choosing the model matters to you,
[self-host Casama](https://casama.ai/self-hosted), which is free.

## Questions

### Which AI agents work with OpenRouter?

Any agent that takes an OpenAI-style endpoint can usually use OpenRouter. Self-hosted Casama has
OpenRouter as one of its built-in providers.

### Can I use my ChatGPT subscription with an AI agent?

Some agents can sign in with it: OpenClaw, Rakazo, Agent Zero and self-hosted Casama say so, and
nanobot can use a Codex sign-in. Check the plan's own limits.

### Is a local model good enough for an agent?

For short, routine tasks, often yes. For long tasks with many steps, hosted models are still
stronger. See [can AI agents run on local models](https://casama.ai/learn/can-ai-agents-run-on-local-models).

# Which AI agents can run tasks on a schedule?

Most AI agents can now run a task on a schedule, such as "every weekday at 9, summarize my inbox". They differ in four ways: what else can start a task, how many schedules you get, whether your own computer has to stay on, and whether a scheduled task still asks before risky steps. A few go further and reach out first without a schedule.

Updated 2026-11-18. Page: https://casama.ai/learn/which-ai-agents-run-tasks-on-a-schedule

## The list

| Agent | What can start a task |
|---|---|
| **Casama** | Schedules, webhooks, email, calendar events, check-ins |
| **OpenClaw** | Schedules, event triggers, webhooks |
| **Hermes Agent** | Schedules set up in plain language |
| **Rakazo** | Schedules, email, webhooks, GitHub events, watched changes |
| **MausBot** | Schedules, webhooks, app events |
| **OpenBot** | Schedules, at most every 15 minutes, up to 20 |
| **Agent Zero** | Scheduled tasks: cron, one-time or by hand |
| **NanoClaw** | One-time or cron tasks |
| **nanobot** | Time, interval or cron schedules, command triggers and long-running goals |
| **n8n** | Schedules and app triggers |
| **Lindy** | Schedules, plus email, Slack, calendar and meeting events |
| **Manus** | Schedules and events: 2 on Free, 20 on Pro |
| **Grok Bot** | Schedules and some events |
| **Claude Cowork and Duet** | Scheduled tasks; Duet sends a morning brief |
| **Meta Muse** | Schedules and events |
| **Hark Pro** | Scheduled tasks |
| **ChatGPT Dots** | Looks for ways to help when idle; schedules aren't described |
| **Instinct** | Reviews say it texts or calls you first |

Checked on November 18, 2026, from each product's own pages; the sources are at the end. We make
Casama.

## Four things that differ

### 1. What starts a task

A clock is the simplest trigger. Events are often more useful: a new email, a meeting ending, a
webhook from another app, a change on a page. Lindy, Rakazo and Casama start tasks from email and
calendar or meeting events. n8n has app triggers for hundreds of apps.

### 2. Limits

Some products cap schedules. Manus allows 2 on Free and 20 on Pro. OpenBot allows up to 20, run at
most every 15 minutes. Check the cap before you plan a dozen daily reports.

### 3. Whether your computer must stay on

An agent installed on your laptop only runs its schedule while the laptop is awake. MausBot says
free bots stop when your computer is off, and nanobot has to be kept running for chat apps and
schedules. Hosted agents, and self-hosted ones on an always-on server, keep going.

### 4. Whether a scheduled task still asks

A task that runs at 3 a.m. has nobody watching. Anthropic advises against scheduling Claude tasks
that send, buy or do things that are hard to undo. Look for an agent whose approvals still apply to
scheduled runs, with the request waiting for you rather than the step going ahead.

## Agents that reach out first

A schedule does what you told it. A proactive agent notices something and offers. Claude Duet sends
a morning brief. ChatGPT Dots look for ways to help when idle, and unprompted work is read-only.
Reviews say Instinct texts or calls first. Casama bots send a morning brief and suggestions you can
start with one tap.

## Routines in Casama

In Casama a scheduled or triggered task is a routine. You can ask for one in chat ("every weekday
at 9:00, summarize my inbox") or build it in the bot's profile.

- **Triggers:** once at a set time, a repeating schedule or cron expression with a timezone,
  meetings, messages, webhooks, GitHub events and events on your phone.
- **Watchers:** "tell me when" a page, price or delivery changes.
- **An end:** stop on a date or after a number of runs.
- **The same approvals:** what a routine does still goes through the bot's usual approvals, so a
  3 a.m. run waits for you before sending an email. A run that waits costs nothing.
- **Costs:** each routine lists its recent runs with what each cost, and the bot's daily budget
  still applies.

Routines run on Casama Cloud or on your own server, so they don't need your laptop. See the
[routines guide](https://docs.casama.ai/guide/routines).

## Questions

### What is a proactive AI assistant?

One that starts work without being asked: a morning brief, a reminder it thought of, an offer to
handle something it noticed. Schedules are the simple version; check-ins and suggestions go further.

### Can an AI agent send me a daily summary?

Yes. Almost every agent above can. Point it at your inbox, calendar or a set of sites and give it a
time.

### Do scheduled AI tasks cost money when nothing happens?

Each run that calls a model costs model usage, even if it finds nothing to do. Pick a schedule that
matches how often things change.

## Related questions

- [Which AI agents ask before they act?](https://casama.ai/learn/which-ai-agents-ask-before-they-act)
- [What is an AI teammate?](https://casama.ai/learn/what-is-an-ai-teammate)

# Why give an AI agent its own computer?

An AI agent with its own computer works apart from your devices, keeps going when you close your laptop, keeps its files and sign-ins between tasks, and can be rolled back when it makes a mistake.

Updated 2026-11-18. Page: https://casama.ai/learn/why-give-an-ai-agent-its-own-computer

## Three places an agent can work

| | Your own computer | A browser session | A computer of its own |
|---|---|---|---|
| Setup | Install an app | None | None, or self-host |
| Can reach your files | Yes | No | Only what you share |
| Works while you're away | Only if your machine stays on | For a short session | Yes |
| Keeps files and sign-ins | Yes | Usually not | Yes |
| If it makes a mistake | It happened on your machine | Limited to the session | Limited to its machine; restore a checkpoint |
| Can run code and install tools | Yes | No | Yes |

## What an own computer makes possible

- **Long work.** A task that takes an hour doesn't need your laptop open for an hour.
- **Real tools.** A full machine has a shell, a file system and a browser, so the agent can
  download a file, convert it, run a script on it and upload the result.
- **A working state.** The half-finished spreadsheet, the cloned repository and the signed-in
  session are still there next time.
- **Containment.** The agent can't read your documents or your saved passwords, because they
  aren't on its machine.
- **Undo.** A snapshot before a risky command lets you put everything back.
- **Watching.** You can open the computer's screen, see what the agent is doing, and take over.

## The costs

- **Money.** A computer that runs costs something per hour. Good systems put it to sleep when
  idle and wake it with everything intact.
- **Sign-ins.** The agent's computer isn't signed in to your accounts. You connect apps, or hand
  it logins through a password manager, ideally in a way the AI model never sees.
- **Bot checks.** Some websites challenge cloud browsers. Being able to take over for a moment
  helps.

## One computer for all agents, or one each?

Some products give every agent its own machine. Others run all of a person's agents on one shared
machine. One each means a research agent that installs odd software can't break the assistant that
handles your mail, and each can be limited to the sites it needs.

*Diagram: Two diagrams side by side. On the left, three bots all feed into one shared computer that holds one set of files and a shared setup, so what one bot does can affect the others. On the right, three bots each have their own computer with their own files and sign-ins, so each bot is walled off from the others, as in Casama.*

Bots on one shared computer share its files and setup. In Casama, each bot works on its own computer.

## How Casama does it

Every Casama bot works on its own isolated Linux machine with a shell, files and a browser, and
optionally a full desktop. Computers sleep when idle and wake with everything intact. You can watch
one live, take control, and restore a checkpoint taken before a destructive command. Logins from
1Password or Bitwarden are filled in on the way out and never shown to the model. If you'd rather a
bot used your own machine for a task, you can lend it through the desktop app, where high-risk
actions always ask.

## Related questions

- [How do AI agents work?](https://casama.ai/learn/how-do-ai-agents-work)
- [What is a computer use agent, and which let you take over?](https://casama.ai/learn/what-is-a-computer-use-agent)
- [Is it safe to give an AI agent access to my email?](https://casama.ai/learn/is-it-safe-to-give-an-ai-agent-access-to-my-email)

Join the waitlist at https://casama.ai/waitlist (Casama Cloud is invite-only for now), or run it on your own server: https://docs.casama.ai/self-hosting/

# Casama's monthly email

What shipped, what's coming next and one good way to put your AI teammates to work. One email a month at most.

Updated 2026-11-19. Page: https://casama.ai/newsletter

Sign up with the form at https://casama.ai/newsletter. You'll get an email with a link to confirm.

## What you get

Once a month, a short email from the people who make Casama:

- **What shipped.** The new things in the apps and on Casama Cloud, in plain words, with a link to the full [changelog](https://casama.ai/changelog) if you want every detail.
- **What's coming next.** What we're working on now, so you can tell us early if it's what you need.
- **One way to use it.** A bot, routine or set-up from the [gallery](https://gallery.casama.ai) or from people using Casama, with the steps to try it yourself.
- **Self-hosting notes.** When a release matters to people who [run Casama on their own server](https://casama.ai/self-hosted), such as a security fix or an update to the computer image, the email says so.

It comes from news@news.casama.ai. Replies go to a person at hello@casama.ai, so you can answer any issue with a question or an idea.

## How signing up works

Enter your email above and press **Subscribe**. We send one email with a link. Open it and press **Confirm**, and you're on the list. A short welcome email follows with what to expect. Until you confirm, we don't keep your address, and if you never open the link you won't hear from us again.

Confirmation links work for seven days. If yours has expired, sign up again and we'll send a new one.

## What we never do

- We never add you without asking. Making a Casama account doesn't sign you up.
- We never sell or share the list. It's kept with [Resend](https://resend.com), the service that sends the emails, and used for nothing else.
- We don't track opens or clicks in these emails.
- We send one email a month at most, plus the confirmation and a short welcome when you sign up.

## Stopping

Every email has an **Unsubscribe** link at the bottom. One click and you're off the list, with no reason needed. You can also reply to any issue and ask, or write to [privacy@casama.ai](mailto:privacy@casama.ai) to have your address removed completely. More about how we handle your data is in the [privacy policy](https://casama.ai/privacy).

## Other ways to follow along

- The [blog](https://casama.ai/blog/) has longer posts about how Casama works and what we learned building it. It has an [RSS feed](https://casama.ai/blog/rss.xml) too.
- The [changelog](https://casama.ai/changelog) lists every change, version by version, with its own [feed](https://casama.ai/changelog/rss.xml).
- The code and every discussion are on [GitHub](https://github.com/stackwares/casama).
